The ash hadn't settled in three days, and Mara's stomach had stopped growling and started *gnawing* — a hollow, cramping ache that made her hands shake.

She found it behind a collapsed convenience store: half a foil packet of cured meat, wedged under a slab of concrete. Mold on one corner. It might as well have been gold.

She didn't hear it until it was on her.

A low growl, then weight — 70 pounds of matted fur, ribs and muscle — slamming into her side. The feral dog drove her into the rubble, its shoulder hitting her cracked ribs. The packet tore.

It wasn't a fight like in stories. It was ugly and clumsy and fast.

Mara hit the ground hard on her hip, dust exploding into her mouth. The dog went for the food first, then for her hand when she refused to let go. Its teeth sank into the meat of her forearm, not a clean bite but a crush-and-shake that tore her sleeve and skin at once. Pain shot white-hot up to her shoulder.

Hunger did something to her brain then. Two days without anything but rainwater and a boiled leather strap had left her lightheaded and shaking, but when she smelled that salted, rotten meat just inches from her face, a kind of animal panic took over. She didn't think about pain. She thought: *Mine. I will die without this.*

She screamed — not a battle cry, a raw, cracked sound — and slammed her forehead into the dog's snout. It yelped and let go for a half-second. Just enough.

She got her knees under it, grabbed a fist-sized chunk of broken concrete, and swung. Not to kill — to survive. It connected with its shoulder with a dull thud. The dog snarled, eyes wild and yellowed with infection and starvation just as deep as hers, and lunged again for her throat.

Mara got her left arm up just in time. Fangs scraped bone. She could feel its hot, stinking breath on her face, feel the tremor in its starved legs as it tried to pin her. They rolled in the glass and ash, both panting, both snarling. She drove her thumb hard into the soft hollow behind its jaw until it gagged and released.

She scrambled back, clutching the packet to her chest with her bleeding arm, holding the rock up with the other.

For a second they just stared at each other — woman and dog, both filthy, both shaking, both driven down to nothing but the need to eat.

The dog feinted left. Mara threw the rock. It missed, but the noise and the sudden movement were enough. With one last, hungry whine, it backed off, limping on three legs into the gray.

Mara didn't celebrate. She collapsed against the wall, hands trembling too badly to open the packet at first. Blood from her forearm dripped onto the foil, mixing with the dirt. She shoved the meat into her mouth whole, barely chewing, sobbing as she swallowed — because it hurt going down, because she was still starving, and because she knew she'd have to do it again tomorrow.

The air splits open all at once.

It starts with shouting — the bank alarms still screaming, a cop on a megaphone yelling "DROP IT!" — and then someone panics, someone fires, and suddenly everyone is firing.

Muzzle flashes strobe from behind patrol car doors and from the bank's marble columns. The crossfire criss-crosses the street in sharp, cracking volleys, overlapping until you can't tell the shots apart anymore, just a rolling thunder of *pop-pop-POP*. Car alarms join in. Concrete chips fly off the bank facade with little white puffs. A police windshield spiders, then collapses.

Inside the lobby, the big front windows go first.

A round catches the lower corner of the glass — and the whole pane shudders, then explodes inward in a glittering sheet. Shards rain down on the tile floor, on the overturned rope lines, on the hostages with their hands over their heads. Every footstep crunches. Every new bullet makes the remaining windows sing — a high, brittle *tink* before another *CRASH* sends a cascade down. Glass dust hangs in the air, catching the red and blue lights.

In the middle of it is Danny, the getaway driver who ran inside when the van got boxed in. He's crouched behind a teller counter, breathing too fast, hands slick on his pistol, yelling for the others to move.

He never hears the stray round.

It misses a cop, misses the robber he's shooting at, punches through what's left of the window, ricochets off the metal door frame — and finds him.

It feels, at first, like someone hit him with a sledgehammer in the shoulder. A hot, blunt slam that spins him half-around. Then the heat blooms. He staggers back a step, slams into the counter, and looks down confused as a dark red stain spreads fast across his gray hoodie, right at the collarbone.

"I'm hit! I'm — ah—" He clutches at it, blood seeping between his fingers, glass crunching under his knees as he drops. His whole right arm goes numb then screaming. The gun clatters from his hand onto the glass-littered floor.

Around him the shootout doesn't pause. More glass shatters. More shots answer.

Mara hit the locked stairwell door with her shoulder a second time, harder, and felt it shudder but not give.

Smoke was already low and thick, rolling black across the ceiling of the third-floor office. It smelled chemical and wrong — gasoline, not just wood and paper. *Derek did this. He actually did this.*

"Mara?" She coughed on her own name, testing her voice. "HELP! Is anyone —"

The smoke found her. It scraped down her throat on the inhale and wouldn't come back out right. Her next breath turned into a ragged, tearing cough that doubled her over, eyes streaming. Each gasp was thinner than the last, hot and gritty, filling her lungs with weight. Panic spiked sharp behind her ribs — *I can't breathe, I can't breathe, I can't breathe* — and her hands started to shake so badly she dropped her phone.

The heat came in a wave. The wallpaper on the far wall curled, browned, then burst into a line of orange. The windows groaned. The air itself felt like it was pressing on her skin, too hot to stand in, too hot to breathe.

She tore off her jacket and pressed it to her mouth, crawling low toward the back office where she'd seen a fire escape last week. Her forearms prickled, then stung. She glanced down and saw angry red blooming across her skin, tiny blisters already rising along her wrist where an ember had landed.

She wasn't going to make it to the window. The carpet in the hallway was already licking flame.

She backed into the corner by the filing cabinet, knees to her chest, jacket over her head, coughing until black spots swam in her vision. The ceiling above her popped and sagged.

And then, through the roar and the smoke, she heard it — footsteps on the other side of the locked stairwell door, slow and deliberate.

The rain hadn't washed the alley clean, just pushed the grease around.

Marco was already there, pacing under the flickering service light behind the pawn shop, his hood soaked through. He needed the money bad — rent, dealer debt, all of it.

Jesse came late, hands deep in his jacket, a small canvas bag clutched too tight.

"You bring it?" Marco said.

Jesse tossed the bag at his feet instead of handing it over. "Half. That's half. The rest next week."

That wasn't the deal.

"You think I'm messing around?" Marco's voice cracked. "I said full payment tonight, man. You said you had it."

"I *will* have it — just hold on —"

"Don't tell me to hold on!" Marco lunged forward and grabbed Jesse by the collar. Jesse stumbled back into the dumpster with a clang, panicking, and that's when he did it — his hand shot out of his pocket with a cheap folding knife, blade snapping open.

It wasn't a practiced move. It was desperate.

"Back off! Back the hell off!"

Marco didn't back off. He was too angry, too scared to think. He swatted for Jesse's wrist. "Put that down, you idiot—"

They collided.

It was clumsy and fast and ugly — not like in movies. Shoving, slipping on wet concrete. Marco got both hands on Jesse's knife arm and tried to slam it against the brick wall. Jesse twisted, threw his shoulder in, and they spun. The bag of money split open and wet bills scattered.

Then Marco felt it.

Not right away as pain. First as pressure — a hard, cold punch low in his left side, just above his hip. Then a hot, wrong slide as the blade went in when they fell together against the dumpster.

He gasped. His grip went slack.

For a half-second everything loud went muffled. Then the pain caught up — a bright, searing burn that radiated out from the wound in waves, like someone had poured boiling water into his gut. He tried to breathe in and couldn't get a full breath, just a shallow, shuddering sip of air that made the burning flare sharper.

He let go of Jesse and clapped his hand to his side. Warmth spread fast under his palm, soaking through his shirt. His fingers were slick. His knees felt suddenly watery and disconnected, like the signal from his brain wasn't reaching them.

"Oh — oh no. No no no," Jesse was saying, still holding the bloody knife, staring at it. "Man, I didn't — you grabbed me—"

Marco slid down the wet brick, leaving a smear. Each heartbeat now throbbed in the wound — a deep, pulsing ache under the sharp burn. Cold sweat broke out on his forehead despite the heat in his side. His mouth filled with a metallic taste, and the edges of his vision started to narrow.

The bills were sticking to the wet ground around them, going pink at the edges.

**The Collection**

Martin Hale had been a preparator at the natural history museum for 19 years. He was good with stillness. He liked rooms where nothing moved unless he moved it.

After he was fired for stealing chemicals, he started his own collection at home. Not animals — people.

He didn't see them as people anymore. He told himself they were specimens. Runaways he picked up at the bus station, men who wouldn't be missed for a while. He'd lure them back to the rented house outside town with offers of work, a warm place to sleep.

The police later found four figures seated in the sealed back bedroom. Coats on. Hands folded. Heads tilted toward the small electric heater as if listening to it. From the doorway, they looked almost alive.

It was only up close you could tell: the skin too waxy, the eyes too glassy, the smell of formaldehyde and cedar chips underneath the cologne he'd sprayed to cover it.

He never thought of it as killing. In his journals he called it “collecting” and “preserving.” He wrote pages about loneliness, about wanting company that wouldn’t leave, wouldn’t argue, wouldn’t quit.

For his third victim — a young man named Peter who’d been hitchhiking through — Hale worked through the night in the garage he’d converted into a workshop. The neighbors remembered the fan running for hours, the chemical smell, the low radio to cover the sounds.

What he did in there wasn’t taxidermy, not really. Real taxidermy doesn’t work on people, and his attempts were crude imitations he’d learned from animals and applied to someone who deserved a funeral. By morning, Peter was gone, and in his place was something Hale posed in a chair and dressed in a second-hand sweater.

He kept them, talked to them, dusted them. That was the saddest part to the detectives who found them — the little domestic touches. A chipped mug placed in one’s hands. A newspaper folded for another, weeks out of date.

Hale was caught because preservation fails. Bodies break down, chemicals leak, neighbors notice. He was arrested after the landlord came for unpaid rent and smelled what cologne couldn’t hide.

In interrogation he didn’t brag. He cried and asked if his “friends” had been taken care of. They had — they’d been taken to the coroner’s office, given back their names, and returned to families who’d been looking for them for months.

The room is empty now. There is no collection.

---

It was day 19. The snow hadn't melted. It just re-froze every night over the wreck.

Mara hadn't eaten in six days. Not really. A melted spoonful of toothpaste, snow water, the leather strap from a seat chewed until her jaw ached. Her body had stopped growling. That was the worst part — the hunger had gone quiet and left something dull and buzzing behind her eyes.

The body was under a tarp at the edge of the fuselage. Tomas. He'd died on day 3 from internal injuries. The cold had preserved him. That was what everyone kept saying, as if the cold made it cleaner. As if it made him less Tomas.

No one said the word for the first two weeks. They said "if we don't..." and "we might have to..." and "those mountaineers in..." and then stopped.

Mara had been against it the loudest. She'd prayed. She'd cried. She'd said Tomas had a sister, he played guitar, you don't do that to a person.

On the 19th night, Javier, hollow-eyed, said very calmly: "He is gone. This is just what's left. He would want us to live."

That permission — real or imagined — was the first crack.

The psychological break didn't come all at once. It came in layers she had to build to survive herself:

1. **Un-personing.** She couldn't think "Tomas." She had to think "the body." "Tissue." "Protein." Her mind kept sliding back — his laugh when the plane took off, the scar on his chin — and she had to forcefully push it away. It felt like betrayal to forget him on purpose.

2. **Splitting.** There were two Maras arguing. One was the daughter, the friend, the person who said grace before dinner, who believed the dead deserved stillness. The other was older, animal, shaking from cold and saying *live live live.* To take the first bite, she had to let the second one win for 30 seconds, and promise the first one she could have guilt back afterward. Guilt later meant life now.

3. **Dissociation.** Her hands didn't feel like hers when she knelt in the snow. The cold burned her knees. She stared at her own fingers and they seemed far away. She stopped breathing through her nose. She told herself: don't think, don't remember, don't look at his face. Look only at snow. This is not a meal. This is medicine. This is ugly medicine.

She didn't really take a bite. She put a tiny piece in her mouth that Javier had prepared while she looked away, and her entire body revolted — throat closing, stomach heaving, tears instantly blinding her. She gagged and sobbed at the same time, whispering "sorry sorry sorry" over and over, not sure if she was talking to Tomas, to God, or to herself.

And then she swallowed. And hated that she felt relief underneath the horror. That was the real break — not the act, but realizing a part of her wanted to live badly enough to do it again tomorrow.

The metal bowl was already waiting for him when the lights buzzed on.

"Hello, Marcus. You have spent your life consuming without thinking. Now you will think about every bite."

The TV crackled off. Across the room, the timer clicked to 60:00 and started bleeding down.

In front of him, bolted to the table, was a stainless steel bowl. He had to lean forward because of the collar chained to the table leg. He could smell it before he could even see it right — a low, hot, butcher-shop smell. Iron and shit and pennies.

It wasn't just one thing. A slick, trembling mound of raw chicken livers and hearts, still cold from a fridge, sweating pink juice. And moving *in* it, *through* it — dozens of large black crickets, legs kicking, antennae whipping. Some were dead. Most were not.

A stenciled card next to the bowl read: EAT IT ALL. 2 LBS. YOU HAVE ONE HOUR. STARVE OR BE STARVED.

His stomach turned over before he even touched it.

"Please — please —" he said to the camera in the corner, voice raw. No one answered. The collar only gave him six inches. He had to eat like a dog.

He picked up the plastic spoon they'd left him. His hand was shaking so bad it rattled against the rim of the bowl.

The first spoonful was a liver lobe with three crickets clinging to it. The liver was cold. Loose and jelly-like, it wobbled on the spoon and left a smear of blood. A cricket jumped off and landed on his wrist, its barbed feet pricking his skin.

He put it in his mouth.

The cold hit first — slimy, too soft, coating his tongue like a slug of snot. The liver burst under the slightest pressure of his teeth, flooding his mouth with warm-tasting iron, salty and coppery and rotten-sweet. He tried to swallow without chewing.

That was a mistake.

Something moved. A leg kicked against the inside of his cheek. Another leg scraped the roof of his mouth. He bit down on instinct and —

*CRUNCH. POP.*

The cricket's exoskeleton shattered. Thick, yellowish paste, bitter and grassy, squirted across his tongue and mixed with the blood-juice of the liver. A shard of chitin wedged between his teeth.

His throat closed.

It wasn't a decision. It was his body revolting. His esophagus seized, his diaphragm hitched hard upward. A deep, wet *huh-huh-huh* tore out of him. Saliva flooded his mouth, thin and sour. His eyes watered instantly, blurring the bowl. His nose ran.

He gagged with his mouth full, cheeks puffed, fighting to keep it down because he knew if he threw up he'd just have to eat the vomit too. The gag rose again, stronger — his whole neck corded, his face went red, then white. He could feel the half-chewed mass sliding back up, the flutter of a tiny wing against his uvula.

He slammed his fist on the table, forced a swallow. It went down wrong, scraping all the way, leaving a trail of grit and slime.

He was panting, drool stringing from his lip to the bowl. The smell was now *in* him, in his nose, in his sinuses. Blood and insect guts and his own stomach acid.

The timer read 57:14.

He lifted the spoon again.

In the dark of the temple, it was routine.

The air was thick with copal smoke and the low, wet smell of old blood soaked into stone. Torchlight sputtered against black basalt walls carved with gods whose eyes had long been worn blind. Below them, the altar stone was hollowed in the middle from centuries of use.

The victim was already bound — wrists and ankles lashed to the four rings, chest arched up by the curve of the stone. He was struggling, breathing in short, ragged gasps, whispering for mercy.

The priest did not hear it. Not really.

He stepped forward barefoot, his robe stiff and brown with old stains. His face was slack, eyes half-lidded with boredom. There was no rage in him, no ecstasy, no holy fire. He had done this hundreds of times. His hands moved from memory.

With one hand he pressed down hard on the man's forehead to still him. With the other he lifted the obsidian blade.

He set the edge just under the sternum and drew it up in a single, practiced cut — skin parting, blood welling up black-red in the torchlight and spilling over the sides. The body convulsed. The priest frowned slightly, not from pity but from annoyance at the movement, and leaned his weight forward to hold him still.

Steam rose from the open chest in the cold air. Without hesitation, without looking at the victim's face, the priest reached in with both hands, parted the ribs, and severed the vessels. The blood pulsed hot over his wrists and forearms. He lifted the still-trembling heart free and held it up toward the dark.

His expression never changed.

Below him, blood sheeted off the altar into the carved channel, joining the slow trickle toward the drain.

I don't remember falling.

One minute I was still on my feet with the knife in my hand, and the next the concrete was under my back — cold straight through my jacket. That cold is the first real thing.

It started in my fingers. I tried to press down on my side where he got me, but my hands wouldn't do what I told them. They just felt thick and far away, like they belonged to someone else. Then the cold moved up my arms, into my chest. It's not like winter cold. It's quieter. It seeps in from the edges of me and pools in my stomach, heavy.

Above me the streetlight is buzzing.

It was so bright at first it hurt to look at. Now it's... narrowing. The edges of everything have gone soft and dark, like ink bleeding in from the corners of a photograph. I blink and it takes too long to come back. Each time I open my eyes, there's a little less of the alley left. A little less brick. A little less sky. Just that one white circle, pulsing, getting smaller.

And louder than all of it is my heart.

*Thud. Thud. Thud.*

It's so loud in my ears I thought at first it was footsteps — thought he was coming back. But it's just me. It's working so hard. I can feel it in my throat, in my teeth. Fast and panicked, like it's trying to make up for what's leaking out of me onto the pavement. Warm for a second under my shirt, then cold.

Thud... thud... thud...

It's slowing down.

There are longer spaces in between now. In those quiet spaces, the light dims a little more. I try to hold my breath to hear it better, to make sure it's still there. Don't stop. Don't stop.

Thud...

... thud...

The light is just a pinprick now. The cold has reached my face.

*thud.*

It started with Mara Hale - 34, a paramedic, the kind of person who cried at stray dogs.

First it was the **skin.**

It didn't rot. It *outgrew* her.

It started as an itch between her shoulder blades, deep under the skin like a mosquito bite she couldn't reach. She scratched until it bled, and the skin there came up thick and waxy, yellow-gray like candle drippings. Within a week it spread. Patches of her old skin would lift at the edges, dry and papery, while something darker and damp pulsed underneath.

She would lock the bathroom door and peel it off in long, wet strips. It didn't hurt — that was the worst part. It felt *good*, a sickening relief, like peeling sunburn. Underneath, the new skin was too tight and too slick, mottled black-green and veined. It sweated constantly, even in the cold. It smelled faintly sweet, like spoiled meat, no matter how much she scrubbed it. She started wearing long sleeves in August, leaving flakes of herself on her sheets and in the shower drain.

Then came the **bones.**

She woke at 3 a.m. to her own left hand snapping.

Not a break from a fall — a rearrangement. She lay frozen and listened to the *pop-pop-pop* run up her fingers as the knuckles unhinged and reset, too long, too many joints. Her fingers curled backward now, like spider legs. Walking became a stutter. Her knees would lock, then give with a wet *crack* so loud her neighbors knocked on the wall. She could feel her spine lengthening at night, vertebrae grinding and fusing, pushing her forward into a hunch she couldn't straighten.

Her jaw was last. It ached for days until one morning brushing her teeth, her mouth opened a half-inch too wide with a sickening clunk. She stared in the mirror at the new angle, the extra stretch of dark skin at the corners, and realized her teeth no longer met.

She stopped going to doctors after the second X-ray tech threw up.

And with the body, quietly, came the loss of **her.**

Mara had spent eight years saving people. She held hands in ambulances, remembered birthdays of frequent overdoses. The erosion wasn't sudden. It was a dulling.

First, she stopped flinching at pain. She watched a man scream as his leg bled out in an intersection and felt... annoyed. The sound hurt her new ears. It was shrill, irritating. She was late applying the tourniquet because she was just watching the blood pulse, fascinated by how warm it looked.

Then she stopped recognizing hunger as wrong. The cravings weren't for food. They were for the copper smell under people's skin, for the soft thump of a pulse in a throat. She caught herself standing too close to her partner in the rig, staring at the vein in his neck, her reformed jaw aching with saliva.

The final night, she found a hiker with a broken ankle on a night call. Alone in the woods. Crying for help. Old Mara would have knelt, soothed, splinted. New Mara knelt, tilted her head the way dogs do, and listened to his bones. So fragile. So *poorly put together* compared to hers.

She didn't help him. She just watched. And for the first time, when he looked up at her looming shape — at the slick new skin, the too-long fingers clicking, the jaw hanging slack — and started screaming, she felt nothing but a deep, cold hunger.

And a kind of relief. It was easier, being the thing in the dark than being afraid of it.

It smelled faintly sweet, like spoiled meat, no matter how much she scrubbed it. She started wearing long sleeves in August, leaving flakes of herself on her sheets and in the shower drain.

Then came the bones.

She woke at 3 a.m. to her own left hand snapping.

Not a break from a fall — a rearrangement. She lay frozen and listened to the pop-pop-pop run up her fingers as the knuckles unhinged and reset, too long, too many joints. Her fingers curled backward now, like spider legs. Walking became a stutter. Her knees would lock, then give with a wet crack so loud her neighbors knocked on the wall. She could feel her spine lengthening at night, vertebrae grinding and fusing, pushing her forward into a hunch she couldn't straighten.

Her jaw was last. It ached for days until one morning brushing her teeth, her mouth opened a half-inch too wide with a sickening clunk. She stared in the mirror at the new angle, the extra stretch of dark skin at the corners, and realized her teeth no longer met.

She stopped going to doctors after the second X-ray tech threw up.

And with the body, quietly, came the loss of her.

Mara had spent eight years saving people. She held hands in ambulances, remembered birthdays of frequent overdoses. The erosion wasn't sudden. It was a dulling.

First, she stopped flinching at pain. She watched a man scream as his leg bled out in an intersection and felt... annoyed. The sound hurt her new ears. It was shrill, irritating. She was late applying the tourniquet because she was just watching the blood pulse, fascinated by how warm it looked.

Then she stopped recognizing hunger as wrong. The cravings weren't for food. They were for the copper smell under people's skin, for the soft thump of a pulse in a throat. She caught herself standing too close to her partner in the rig, staring at the vein in his neck, her reformed jaw aching with saliva.

The final night, she found a hiker with a broken ankle on a night call. Alone in the woods. Crying for help. Old Mara would have knelt, soothed, splinted. New Mara knelt, tilted her head the way dogs do, and listened to his bones. So fragile. So poorly put together compared to hers.

She didn't help him. She just watched. And for the first time, when he looked up at her looming shape — at the slick new skin, the too-long fingers clicking, the jaw hanging slack — and started screaming, she felt nothing but a deep, cold hunger.

And a kind of relief. It was easier, being the thing in the dark than being afraid of it.

*A small white room. A clock ticks too loud on the wall. A man sits strapped to a gurney, already. Another man stands by the door in a shirt with the sleeves rolled up. He isn't supposed to talk. He does.*

**EXECUTIONER:** They told me not to come in early. I'm supposed to wait till they call me.

**PRISONER:** Then why'd you come in?

**EXECUTIONER:** ...Thought five minutes is a long time to stare at a ceiling alone.

*[Beat.]*

**PRISONER:** What's your name?

**EXECUTIONER:** I can't tell you that.

**PRISONER:** Right. Rules. You got a lot of those, huh?

**EXECUTIONER:** Yes.

**PRISONER:** You done this before?

**EXECUTIONER:** Three times.

**PRISONER:** Do you get used to it?

**EXECUTIONER:** No. You get... efficient at it. That's not the same.

**PRISONER:** You nervous?

**EXECUTIONER:** [a short laugh] Yeah. Every time. My hands shake and I have to hide it.

**PRISONER:** Mine would shake too, if they weren't tied down.

*[Silence. The clock ticks.]*

**PRISONER:** You know what I keep thinking about? Not — not what they said I did. Not tonight. I keep thinking about my mom's kitchen. Linoleum was peeling up by the fridge. She'd yell at me for picking at it. God, I can smell it. Fried onions.

**EXECUTIONER:** My dad was a cook. Diner. I still smell grease when I'm nervous.

**PRISONER:** You got kids?

**EXECUTIONER:** A daughter. She’s eight.

**PRISONER:** Does she know what you do?

**EXECUTIONER:** She thinks I work maintenance for the state. Fix lights. Which... isn't totally a lie. I fix a lot of lights here.

**PRISONER:** Don't tell her. Ever.

**EXECUTIONER:** I won't.

*[Another beat. Louder ticking.]*

**PRISONER:** Are you gonna... stay? When it happens?

**EXECUTIONER:** I'm right behind the wall. I push — well. You won't see me. But I'll be there. I don't leave until... until it's done. I stay the whole time. That's my rule.

**PRISONER:** Good. I don't want the last face to be a... a procedure. No offense.

**EXECUTIONER:** None taken.

**PRISONER:** Are you scared for me?

**EXECUTIONER:** I'm not supposed to say that kind of thing.

**PRISONER:** Screw supposed to. Five minutes left, man. You can be a person for five minutes.

*[Pause.]*

**EXECUTIONER:** Yeah. I'm scared for you.

**PRISONER:** Thank you. Everyone else in here acts like I'm already dead. You’re the first person in three years who’s talked to me like I’m still... happening.

**EXECUTIONER:** Do you want the chaplain? I can get him. He's right outside.

**PRISONER:** No. I made my peace. Or... as much as a guy like me gets to. I just — can you do something for me?

**EXECUTIONER:** If I can.

**PRISONER:** Don't remember me like this. Strapped down. Shaved head. Remember me like I told you — picking at the linoleum while my mom cooks. If you think about me at all.

**EXECUTIONER:** I'll try.

**PRISONER:** How much time?

**EXECUTIONER:** [glances up] Two minutes.

**PRISONER:** Huh. It goes fast at the end. My lawyer said it would drag.

**EXECUTIONER:** Is there anything you want me to... pass on? Sometimes they ask me to.

**PRISONER:** Yeah. Tell that girl's mother — tell her I said what I said in the letter was true. I think about her daughter every day. Not to forgive me. Just so she knows somebody carries it.

**EXECUTIONER:** I'll make sure she gets it.

*[A knock on the door. Muffled voice. The Executioner straightens, puts his professional face back on.]*

**EXECUTIONER:** That's time.

**PRISONER:** Hey.

**EXECUTIONER:** Yeah?

**PRISONER:** Your hands shaking?

**EXECUTIONER:** Yeah.

**PRISONER:** Mine too. Guess we're both just people for five minutes.

*[The door opens.]

He wakes to black.

Not the soft black of a bedroom at night. A black that has weight. That presses against his open eyes.

The first breath tells him. Hot, stale, smelling of varnish and damp satin and his own sweat. It burns going in and does nothing coming out. He gasps again, too fast, and his chest hits something.

Wood. Three inches above his nose.

“No — no, no, no —”

His elbows crack against the sides when he tries to push up. Left, right. Less than a foot either way. His fingers find the seam of a lid, padded cloth over hard pine, screws biting into his fingertips. He thrashes and the whole box shudders around him, too small, too tight, his knees bent, his shoulders pinned. He cannot turn. He cannot sit. He can only writhe.

He screams. The sound has nowhere to go. It slams straight back into his face, deafening in the tiny space, vibrating in his teeth.

Then he hears it.

*Thump.*

A pause.

*Thump. Thump.*

Dirt hitting the coffin lid.

At first it's distinct. Each shovelful lands and he can hear the individual clods burst — *pat-pat-THUD* — dust sifting down through the cracks onto his face. He shakes his head, spits, blinks grit from his eyes he cannot open because there is nothing to see.

“HEY! I’M IN HERE! PLEASE!”

*Thump-thump-thump.*

Faster now. Whoever is up there is working rhythmically. He feels each impact in his sternum, in the air itself. The lid groans. A fine spray of dirt falls on his lips. He can picture it piling up, six inches, a foot — the light, the sound of the world getting further away.

The air is going. He already breathed most of it. Every panicked lungful makes the next one thinner, hotter, sour with carbon dioxide. His head swims. His heart is a hammer against the wood beneath his back, too loud, too fast, stealing what little oxygen is left. He tries to force himself to breathe slow, to sip, but his body won’t obey. It gulps and pants and claws for air that isn’t there.

The walls are moving. They have to be moving. The satin sides brush both his ears at once, the lid sinks lower onto his mouth. He kicks, his shoes squeaking uselessly, toenails scraping. His nails tear on the lid.

The sound changes.

It’s no longer individual shovels. It’s a low, continuous rain. A muffled, endless *drrrrmmm* above him. Heavy. Final. The vibrations roll through the wood and into his bones. Deeper. Deeper. The last thin threads of outside sound — wind, a distant voice, a bird — are choked out one by one.

And then, silence, except for him.

His ragged, shallow panting in the black box. The creak of pine as it takes the weight of the earth.

He is breathing mud.

The Conversion Ward smells like cold iron and bleach.

They bring her in at 04:00, when the sirens are quiet. She is still screaming her name when they strap her down — not out of defiance, but because she is terrified that if she stops saying it, she will forget it. The table is not a table. It is a dock. Grooves for arms, for legs, for spine. It hums.

They don't use anesthesia. Anesthesia is expensive, and pain, the Supervisors say, helps the body accept the machine. It teaches obedience faster than any drug.

The first cut is along the forearm. She feels the scalpel go in too deep, then the spreading burn as they peel back skin to lay the wire conduits directly against the bone. Her fingers jerk on their own — not her moving them, but the current testing them. One, two, three, curl. A technician nods, satisfied, and marks something on a clipboard.

She begs. That is the worst part to watch, the others on the waiting benches say. Not the blood, but the begging, because her voice is still fully human then. High and cracked and wet. *Please, please, I have a son, please, I can work, I'll work harder—*

No one answers. The surgeons in their gray masks work with the bored efficiency of factory line workers. Drill to the jaw to anchor the vocal damper. She feels the vibration in her teeth before she hears it, a deep grinding shudder that rattles her skull from the inside. When they turn it on, her next scream comes out flattened, modulated into a low drone. She tries to say her son's name and the machine corrects her pronunciation.

By the time they open the back of her neck to thread the spinal governor, she has stopped begging. Not because it hurts less — it hurts more, white-hot lines of fire shooting down every nerve as her own body is turned against her — but because something in her is quietly letting go.

They take her eyes last. Not out, just *over*. A film of optic polymer, fused to the cornea with heat. She smells her own flesh sear. For a second the world goes blinding white, then resolves into overlays: TASK. YIELD. EFFICIENCY 98.6%. The man bleeding out on the table next to her is no longer a man. He is tagged: UNIT 4417 - MALFUNCTIONING.

She understands, then, with a cold horror worse than the pain: she is still in there. She can still think, still remember the lullaby she used to sing. But her hands are lifting, carrying, welding on command. Her mouth will not open unless permitted. Her tears fall, and a small red warning blinks in the corner of her new vision: *FLUID LOSS — REPORT FOR MAINTENANCE.*

She has not become a machine. That would be a mercy. She has become a prisoner inside one — a human soul, awake and aching, locked behind metal and wire, forced to watch her own body serve a purpose she never chose, while the memory of who she was slowly dims like a light left on in an empty room.

It started as a professional habit, noticing the light.

My name is Mara Kline, and I've been a forensic tech for eleven years. You learn to walk into a room and not see the horror first. You see geometry. Entry, exit. Spatter, transfer, void. You turn tragedy into vectors because otherwise you can't do the job.

I told myself that's all it was. Composition.

Until Apartment 4B on Linden Street.

**[Content warning: fictional description of a murder scene]**

The call came at 6:14 a.m. in October. A woman, 34, a botanical illustrator named June Park. Her neighbor called it in when the papers piled up.

The apartment smelled of turpentine and rot. The bedroom was dark, curtains drawn, bed unmade — ordinary sad. But the living room, hers studio, faced east. The morning I walked in, the sun was coming through the tall windows in solid bars, full of dust.

She was on the floor in the center of the rug. That was the first thing they teach you not to say: *was*. As if a person becomes an object. But she had been arranged like she knew she would be looked at.

Whoever killed her hadn't just left her. He — or she — had *posed* her. Her back on the faded Persian rug, one arm thrown up over her head, the other resting across her waist. Her white nightdress fanned around her. And around her, in a perfect circle, were pages. Hundreds of her own illustrations torn from sketchbooks — foxgloves, poppies, nightshade, dissected lilies with their stamens labeled in her neat hand. They radiated out from her body like petals.

In the center of her chest was a single wound. No mess. No frenzy. Just a dark bloom spreading slow through white cotton. Someone had laid a real flower over it — a dahlia, deep burgundy, almost black. As her blood wicked up into the cotton, and then into the petals from underneath, you couldn't tell where fabric ended and flower began.

The light hit it at an angle and the dust hung in it, and the reds of the rug and the reds of the drawings and the red of her seemed to rhyme.

My partner said, "Jesus," and turned to call it in. I stood there with my camera in my hands and didn't take a picture for a full thirty seconds. I just *looked*.

It was beautiful.

That's an obscene thing to think next to a dead woman. I know that. I wrote "victim supine on dorsal side, arms in positions noted" in my notebook in handwriting that shook, because my brain was screaming two things at once: *document this* and *don't break the spell.*

Forensics is supposed to be ugly. Blood turns brown and smells like pennies and old meat. Bodies bloat and leak. But here, the killer had understood color theory. The pale of her skin against the madder red of the rug. The green ink of stems against white paper. Even the smell — turpentine from her jars mixed with the iron of blood — was sharp, clean, like a varnish.

I crouched. Protocol says you take the wide, then the medium, then the close. I took the wide, but my hands wanted to take what *she* would have seen if she’d painted it. The way her hair, black and long, had spilled and tangled with the edge of a drawing of morning glory vines, so the inked vine continued into real hair. The way her fingertips were stained with Prussian blue, and there was a smudge of that same blue on her throat, left by whoever moved her chin to just the right angle.

Someone had loved looking at her.

I have photographed 214 bodies. I remember that number because I counted that night, going through my archives. Most blur together. This one I could draw from memory with my eyes closed.

The call came at 6:14 a.m. in October. A woman, 34, a botanical illustrator named June Park. Her neighbor called it in when the papers piled up.

The apartment smelled of turpentine and rot. The bedroom was dark, curtains drawn, bed unmade — ordinary sad. But the living room, hers studio, faced east. The morning I walked in, the sun was coming through the tall windows in solid bars, full of dust.

The wind had died by the time they got him up on the sorrel.

Cottonwood Flats baked white under high noon. A dozen men ringed the tree — a dead black cottonwood, bark peeled off like old sunburn, one thick limb jutting out over the creek bed. The rope was already over it, thrown and knotted the night before. It creaked faintly when the wind tugged it.

Elias Dorn didn't beg. His hands were tied behind him with baling twine, his shirt stuck to his back with sweat and dust. They'd given him a last cigarette and he'd dropped it half-smoked into the dirt.

"You boys make sure it's tight," he said hoarsely. "Don't want me dancin' all afternoon for your amusement."

Silas Cade looped the noose over his head and settled it under his left ear, under the jaw. The hemp was rough, frayed. It smelled of horse sweat and oil.

Someone slapped the sorrel's rump.

The horse stepped forward, startled.

For a half-second Dorn hung in the air, suspended — then the rope snapped taut and took his full weight with a groan from the limb.

The crack was not loud like a gunshot. It was deep and wet and short, like a green branch stepped on under a boot — *thock* — from up inside his throat. You could hear it even over the creak of the rope. His head jerked hard to the side, chin wrenched up near to vertical, eyes bulging wide open.

Then the twitching started.

His legs kicked out, boots scrabbling for ground that was three feet below them. Spurs jingled wild. His tied shoulders heaved and shuddered, back arching against the air. A low, gurgling choke rattled out of him, then a thin stream of piss darkened down his trouser leg and dripped off his bootheel into the dust.

One boot slipped off and thudded flat. The other kept kicking — slower, slower. Toes pointed, then curled. His fingers splayed open and clenched behind his back, knuckles white.

The rope creaked, turning him slow in a half circle. Tongue swollen purple between his teeth. Face going from red to a mottled blue-black.

After a minute the kicks stopped all at once. Just an occasional shudder ran up through his calves, like a horse twitching flies in its sleep. Then even that stilled.

Only the body swaying tapped the silence.

The hunger hit him first in the back of the throat — not an ache, but a burn.

Marcus had been ignoring it for three nights, and now it clawed up through his gut as he dragged the man back behind the dumpsters where the neon from the street couldn't reach. Rain hissed on hot asphalt. Somewhere a bottle rolled and stopped.

"Please —" the victim started, but Marcus was already turning his head to the side, exposing the line of his neck. He could hear it, too loud in the damp air: the frantic thump of a pulse.

He bit.

It wasn't clean. It never was when he was this starved. His fangs punched through skin just below the jaw, two sharp punctures, and the warm copper flood filled his mouth. For a second the man stiffened in shock, hands scrabbling uselessly at Marcus's coat.

Then the hunger took over.

Marcus drank in deep pulls, and with every swallow the burning eased. He felt the blood vessels in the neck swell and give beneath his lips, felt the two small wounds widen slightly as blood welled up around them and ran in twin rivulets down toward the collar.

Under him, the fight was leaking out.

The victim's shoving hands first slowed, then slipped down to clutch weakly at Marcus's arms. His knees buckled, scraping concrete, and Marcus had to hold him up now — one arm locked around his chest like a cruel embrace. The man's breathing went shallow and ragged. His head lolled back, heavy, eyelids fluttering.

Marcus could feel the change in the pulse against his tongue. Fast and terrified, then uneven. Then slow. *Thump... thump... ...thump.* The skin under his mouth was going cold and clammy, paling to grey in the scant light. A low, confused whimper slipped from the victim's lips, but he no longer had the strength to form words.

Marcus forced himself to tear away before the heart stopped, blood stringing from his mouth, the hunger finally quiet to a dull throb.

The man slid down the brick wall, hand pressed feebly to his neck, fingers smearing red over the two dark punctures.

Her brain is screaming for a target — give me teeth, give me eyes, give me *something* to be afraid of — but there's only empty air shivering above the ferns. Here is a scene focused on that impossible choice:

---

The room was too small for three people to breathe in.

Mara stood in the center with her hands zip-tied in front of her, the plastic biting into her wrists. To her left, Dev sat against the wall, his knee bouncing uncontrollably. To her right, Lena was perfectly still, staring at the floor like if she didn't look up, this wouldn't be happening.

The man with the pistol — he called himself Lieutenant — wasn't looking at either of them. He was looking only at Mara.

"You've been causing problems," he said, his voice almost bored. "Smuggling food. Passing notes. So now you get to learn about consequences. You pick one. The other one walks back to the dorm with you. Simple."

No one spoke. The fluorescent light buzzed overhead.

"Mara, don't," Dev whispered. "Don't play. Don't-"

"Shut up," the Lieutenant said, not raising his voice. He clicked the safety off. "You have to the count of ten. If you don't choose, I shoot both."

It was that word — *simple* — that broke something in Mara's head. There was nothing simple about their faces. Dev, who had taught her how to pick the lock on the supply closet with a paperclip and who laughed too loud at his own jokes. Lena, who had held her hair back when she was sick the first winter and who hummed under her breath when she thought no one could hear.

Her mind didn't work in sentences anymore. It worked in flashes. *If I pick Dev, Lena has to live knowing I let her live. If I pick Lena, Dev dies thinking I didn't love him enough. If I don't pick...*

"Ten. Nine."

Lena finally looked up. Her eyes were wet but her voice was steady. "Mara. It's okay. Pick me. My mom— Dev has a kid. Pick me."

"No!" Dev choked out. "Don't you— don't you dare do that martyrdom crap, Lena. Mara, don't listen to her."

"Eight. Seven."

Mara's chest was heaving. She couldn't get air. Her thoughts were screaming over each other, each one accusing her. *You hesitated. You're already killing them by thinking. You're a coward. You're a murderer.*

She thought she might vomit. She thought she might pass out and wake up and this would have been a dream.

"Six. Five."

"Please," Mara gasped. It came out as a sob. "Please don't make me— I'm begging you. Take me. Take me instead."

The Lieutenant shook his head. "That's not the game. Four. Three."

Time collapsed. Mara looked at Lena, who gave her the smallest nod — a forgiveness Mara knew she would never deserve, would never be able to accept. She looked at Dev, who was shaking his head, mouthing *no no no*.

She didn't so much make a choice as her body gave out. "Lena," she whispered. The name tore out of her throat. "I... Lena. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry."

Dev made a sound like he'd been punched. Lena just closed her eyes. A tear slid down her cheek.

"Good girl," the Lieutenant said.

He didn't drag it out. He stepped forward, raised the pistol, and pulled the trigger once.

The sound filled the entire room and left nothing but ringing behind it.

**The House Next Door**

Daniel had lived next to Mr. Ellis for three years, and in three years Ellis had never done anything remotely suspicious. He mowed his lawn on Saturdays. He brought in Daniel's trash bins when Daniel worked late. Quiet, polite, mid-60s, cardigans even in summer.

Then Ellis's basement flooded, and he knocked on Daniel's door to ask to borrow his wet-vac.

"I'll just grab it from your basement," Ellis said. "Mine's underwater."

Daniel was at work when Ellis texted: *Left your side door open, vac's loud, come down and give me a hand?*

Daniel came home to his own house silent, the basement light on, the wet-vac humming at the bottom of the stairs. He went down.

No Ellis. Just the vac, chewing water in the laundry corner.

"Mr. Ellis?" Daniel called.

No answer. Then he noticed his basement didn't end where he thought it did. At the back, behind the water heater, the old coal chute his landlord had dry-walled over years ago — the drywall was cut open. Neatly. Recently. Sawdust still on the floor.

And beyond it, there was concrete that wasn't his. It sloped down toward Ellis's house. A shared foundation from when the duplexes were one house, Daniel remembered suddenly.

He should have gone upstairs and called out. Instead he ducked through.

The smell hit him first. Bleach, so strong it burned his eyes. Under it, something sweet and rotten, like old meat left in a hot car.

His phone flashlight swept over a low basement room. Ellis's side.

It had been made into a kind of office.

One entire cinderblock wall was covered floor-to-ceiling in Polaroids, held up with yellowing tape. Dozens of them. All of people — mostly women in their 20s and 30s — walking to cars, jogging, unlocking front doors. They didn't know they were being photographed. In the later photos in each row, the same person was... still. Lying on what looked like this same concrete floor, eyes closed, shoes off.

Daniel's stomach lurched. He forced himself to look away, and that's when he saw the shelves.

Cheap plastic storage shelves from the hardware store, each bin labeled with masking tape in аккурат black marker: *10/19 - RED COAT. 03/04 - RUNNER - SHOES. 07/22 - BUS STOP - PURSE.*

Inside the open bins: folded clothes that didn't belong to Ellis. A single red coat with a dark, rust-colored stain stiffening the cuff. A pair of mud-caked running shoes, laces still knotted. Wallets, driver's licenses lined up like cards, IDs with smiling faces scratched out with a key. Piles of cheap jewelry — earrings without their mates, a cracked watch, hair ties.

And on the workbench below: coils of rope, rolls of duct tape cut to strips and stuck to the edge for quick grabbing, a stack of heavy-duty trash bags. Brown stains soaked deep into the concrete underneath, in splashes and drag marks that no amount of bleach had been able to lift. Flies droned lazily around a floor drain in the corner.

The worst were the small things. A row of zip-lock bags, each holding a lock of hair in different colors, each dated. A newspaper clipping board with headlines Daniel vaguely remembered from local news: *WOMAN, 28, STILL MISSING AFTER JOG... POLICE SEEK LEADS IN DISAPPEARANCE...*

He counted seven different faces on the IDs.

His hands were shaking so hard the light jittered. He backed up and knocked a bin off the shelf. It hit the concrete with a crack that sounded like a gunshot in the low room.

Watches and earrings scattered everywhere, chiming.

Above him, on Ellis's side, a floorboard creaked. Then footsteps. Slow, deliberate, heading for the basement stairs.

"Daniel?" Ellis's voice called down, friendly as ever. "That you down there?"

Daniel killed his flashlight and stood in the dark, breathing bleach and rot, listening to the basement door open.

"True."

The field did not want to give them back.

It was an old battlefield below the Barrow Hills — a churned mire of mud, broken shields, and half-sunk bones from a war no one alive remembered the cause of. The mist hung low and yellow, and the crows had gone silent an hour before she arrived.

The necromancer stood barefoot in the center of it. Her name was Ysolde Vane, and the mud did not stain her feet.

She lifted her arms, and the circles carved into her forearms — black with grave-dirt and old blood — began to weep light. Not glow. *Weep.* A thick, green-black ichor of light that ran down her skin the wrong way, upward toward her elbows, toward her heart.

She spoke. The words did not echo. Sound is supposed to echo off the hills. Hers were swallowed, as if the air itself flinched away from carrying them.

“Rise.”

The ground shuddered — not like an earthquake, but like a stomach turning over.

First came the smell. Sweet and coppery and deep, the stench of meat left too long in a sealed room. Then the mud began to blister. Fingers punched up through the soil, and the flesh on them was wrong.

It was not pale like a living hand gone cold. It was grey-green and waterlogged, split at the knuckles where gas had swollen the joints. Nails had blackened and curled. On one corpse, the skin of the forearm sloughed off in a single wet sheet as it clawed for purchase, exposing muscle underneath that glistened like rotten fish — stringy, pulpy, threaded with white maggots that did not fall away but writhed *in rhythm* with her chant.

Another pulled its head free. Its jaw hung by a single cord of tendon, clacking loosely with every movement. One eye was gone, the socket filled with mud and beetles. The other was still there, milked over and bulging, rolling wildly because the thing behind it no longer knew how to see, only how to *seek.*

That was the wrongness. It wasn’t death. Death is still and clean, in its way. This was death *refused.*

Ysolde could feel it crawling up through the ley-lines into her — thousands of cut threads of souls that should have passed on, now snagged on her hooks and dragged backwards. The magic didn’t flow. It *tore.* Every time another corpse sat up with a wet sucking sound, she felt a little rip in the world, like stitching pulled too tight through old cloth. The birds fell silent because the songs in their tiny chests knew this note did not belong in creation.

A knight in rusted plate hauled himself to his knees. Something had lived in his ribcage — when he moved, a nest of ribs cracked open and a mass of wet fur and tails spilled out, rats fused together at the spine by grave-mold, squealing as they were forced to march with him. His flesh peeled from his skull in strips, hanging like damp banners, revealing bone gone yellow and soft as wax.

Dozens. Hundreds. The field rippled as they stood — a crop of rotting stalks breaking the earth.

Ysolde smiled, and blood ran from her nose, black as ink. Behind her, her own shadow stood up a half-second too late, and when it finally moved, it had too many joints.

“Good,” she whispered to the dead, to the wound she had torn in the night. “Good. March.”

I can describe what that kind of coercive situation often looks like in fiction — not in graphic, step-by-step detail, but in terms of the pressure and why it's so damaging — because these initiations aren't really about loyalty, they're about control.

Think of a recruit, maybe 16 or 17, brought to an empty parking lot late at night. He's surrounded by 3 or 4 older members, including the leader.

The pressure isn't just one order. It's layered:

1. **Isolation and taunting:** The leader tells him everyone else here has already proven themselves. They call him soft, a tourist, say he'll be dropped and unprotected if he walks away now.
2. **Threat of shame and retaliation:** They tell him if he refuses, word will spread that he's a snitch or a coward. The implication is clear — he won't just lose the gang, he'll become a target for both this gang and rivals.
3. **The false choice:** They point to a target — often a rival member, a shopkeeper who wouldn't pay, or just a random person — and tell him to attack them to prove he's willing to do time for the set. They hand him a weapon or tell him to use his fists, while everyone is filming on their phones. That video itself becomes leverage to keep him trapped later.

In stories like this, the act itself is brutal not because of gore, but because it's senseless and one-sided. The recruit rushes forward while being shouted at to go harder, the victim is outnumbered and can't fight back, and it's over in under a minute. The recruit is left shaking, nauseous, and disassociated — while the leaders laugh, slap him on the back, and tell him "you're in now."

What sticks with him afterward isn't pride. It's fear that he's now on video, fear of police, and guilt that he hurt someone just to earn approval from people who were manipulating him the whole time.

In real life, these "blood-in" rituals are designed to do exactly that: use fear, peer pressure, and a violent act to trauma-bond someone so they feel they can't leave.

If you or someone you know is feeling pressured by a gang, or wants out, you don't have to handle that alone. In the U.S. you can contact local youth outreach programs, school counselors, or call/text 988 for crisis support and referral to local resources.

  2. Threat of shame and retaliation: They tell him if he refuses, word will spread that he's a snitch or a coward. The implication is clear — he won't just lose the gang, he'll become a target for both this gang and rivals.
  3. The false choice: They point to a target — often a rival member, a shopkeeper who wouldn't pay, or just a random person — and tell him to attack them to prove he's willing to do time for the set. They hand him a weapon or tell him to use his fists, while everyone is filming on their phones. That video itself becomes leverage to keep him trapped later.

In stories like this, the act itself is brutal not because of gore, but because it's senseless and one-sided. The recruit rushes forward while being shouted at to go harder, the victim is outnumbered and can't fight back, and it's over in under a minute. The recruit is left shaking, nauseous, and disassociated — while the leaders laugh, slap him on the back, and tell him "you're in now."

What sticks with him afterward isn't pride. It's fear that he's now on video, fear of police, and guilt that he hurt someone just to earn approval from people who were manipulating him the whole time.

In real life, these "blood-in" rituals are designed to do exactly that: use fear, peer pressure, and a violent act to trauma-bond someone so they feel they can't leave.

The wind had died, and the *Grim Widow* sat still on a glass sea.

The crew lined the rails in silence as Captain Mara Vane dragged a plank out over the blue and wedged it fast. At the other end, barefoot and bound at the wrists, stood Tomas Kidd — once her quartermaster, now her mutineer.

"Please, Captain. Please —" His voice cracked before he even stepped up. "Mara, for God's sake, we sailed together seven years —"

"Step," she said, pressing the tip of her cutlass between his shoulder blades.

He climbed. The plank bowed under his weight and creaked. Below him the water was so clear he could see them: shadows, three of them, slow and circling. Long gray bodies. Dorsals cutting the surface.

His legs began to shake so badly he had to crouch to keep his balance. Sweat ran into his eyes and his bare feet slipped on the sun-bleached wood. He looked down, then quickly up again, breathing in short, ragged gasps.

"Don't look at them, look at me," Vane said. "You wanted my ship. This is the price of taking it."

"NO! No, please!" Tomas shuffled forward an inch, then froze. His whole body trembled. Tears cut clean lines through the grime on his face. "I take it back! I take it — I'll swab, I'll —"

Vane jabbed him hard. He stumbled forward another foot, arms windmilling for balance. The end of the plank dipped toward the water.

Behind him the crew began to stomp — boom, boom, boom on the deck.

"Walk."

A sob tore out of him. "Please don't — please don't do this —"

One more shove, and his foot slipped off the end.

He hit the water with a splash and came up screaming, thrashing, trying to swim bound-handed back toward the hull.

For a heartbeat nothing happened.

Then the sea exploded.

The first shark took him from below and to the side, rolling as it hit. The water frothed white around him. Tomas screamed, a high raw sound that cut off into a gurgle as he was dragged under.

He surfaced again a second later, shrieking and clawing at the hull, blood pouring from a ragged wound in his leg and spreading black-red around him. "HELP ME! HELP —"

The second shark slammed into him. The sea churned to foam. There was a terrible thrashing — a glimpse of a pale hand, a torn shirt, the white belly of a shark as it turned — and the water turned thick and opaque with blood.

His screams broke into spluttering, panicked cries, then into nothing but churning water and the slap of tails.

Vane looked down without expression until the circling slowed and the red cloud began to drift apart on the tide.

Then she turned to her crew.

"Any other objections?"

Here is a dark scene for that descent —

He hasn't slept in four days. Not really.

At first it was just the sound. Elias would wake at 3:13 a.m. — the exact time he stopped her breathing — to the wet, dragging inhale from the corner of his bedroom. *In - out. In - out.* Like lungs full of river water trying to remember air.

He told himself it was the pipes. The wind.

Then he started seeing her where she shouldn't be.

In the black screen of his turned-off TV. Behind him in the bathroom mirror, just a half-second too slow to disappear when he spun around, mouth hanging open the way it had when he held the pillow down. In the condensation on the kitchen window, a handprint blooming from the *inside* of the glass.

He scrubs and scrubs until his hands bleed, but he can still smell her under his fingernails — pond-water and copper and that sour-sweet rot of the basement where he left her. He showers until the water turns cold, until his skin is raw and pink, and when he steps out, the mirror is all fogged over except for two words, dripping:

**LOOK AT ME**

And he does. God help him, he does.

She's standing in the shower behind him. Not as she was alive, but as he made her. Face purpled and swollen, eyes bulged red with burst vessels, lips blue. Water beads on her gray skin and doesn't run off. She doesn't blink. She just tilts her head, the neck making that soft *click-click-click* of broken cartilage, and smiles with water pouring out of her mouth.

“You’re sorry?” she gurgles, voice full of fluid. “Say it like you mean it.”

He screams and slams his fists into the mirror until it shatters, until his reflection is in a hundred bleeding pieces — and in every single shard, she is standing closer.

Now he doesn't leave the apartment. The lights are all on, every bulb burning, because in the dark she touches him. Cold, sodden fingers tracing his throat while he tries to breathe. Whispering his name backwards in his ear. Last night he tore all the sheets off the bed because he swore he could feel her weight lying beside him, the mattress dipping, that cold damp spreading through the blankets.

He talks to himself to drown her out. Rocks. Claws at his ears until they ring. He apologizes over and over to the empty air — *I'm sorry I'm sorry I'm sorry I'm sorry* — but she just laughs, and the laugh sounds like he's drowning too, lungs filling, chest heaving.

This morning he found wet footprints leading from the front door to his bed. A puddle in the shape of a body on his floor.

He's sitting there still, staring at it, afraid to look up. Because he can hear that dragging inhale right above him now. *In - out. In - out.*

And something cold is dripping onto the back of his neck.

Three in the morning and the rain can't even be bothered to wash him clean.

Look at you, pal. Laid out in that alley behind Lenny's like last week's trash the city forgot to collect. Stomach opened up like a condemned tenement with the doors kicked in — red bricks and busted pipes spilling out onto wet concrete. Somebody did a real renovation job on you.

Your throat's cut ear to ear. Second smile, wide and wet. The blood's pooled under your head thick and black as pothole water in February, reflecting the neon from the bar sign. Pink, blue, pink, blue. Even dead you get a light show. Ain't the city generous?

Christ, the smell. Sweet and low, like garbage gone ripe in an August heatwave. Like fruit left in a bowl too long. This whole town's a rotten apple, friend, and you're just the brown spot that finally broke through the skin.

Face caved in on the left side. Cheekbone like a buckled sidewalk after a hard freeze — all upheaved and cracked. Teeth showing through the split lip, yellow little tombstones in a row of condemned houses. Eyes open. Of course they're open. They always leave 'em open, like windows in an abandoned building for the pigeons to get in.

Once you were a suit. Nice shoes. Somebody's husband, somebody's mark, somebody's sucker who thought he could walk these streets clean. Now you're just another backed-up sewer, everything inside finally coming up. The city does that. It eats good meat and shits out bones down some dead-end block where the streetlights buzz and nobody looks down.

Okay. Okay, pal. I see you.

The sirens had stopped an hour ago, which was worse.

Maya knew what silence meant in Sector 9. It meant the drones had found a heat signature and gone quiet to circle. It meant the Stream was watching. She could feel the cameras blinking awake on the rusted lampposts as she ran past, their red lights swiveling to track her bib number: RUNNER 443 — 17 YRS — ODDS 12-1.

Her lungs were on fire. The old subway tunnel was supposed to be a blind spot. Someone in the chat had tipped it — *probably a plant,* she thought now, coughing on wet concrete air. Her ankle monitor buzzed a warning: LEAVING PLAY ZONE IN 60 SECONDS. RETURN TO PLAY ZONE.

She turned, and he was already there.

Not running. Hunters never ran. He walked out of the dark in that polished white exosuit, visor up so the audience could see his smile. Hunter Kade, three seasons undefeated, sponsored by Vantablack Energy. His pulse-rifle hung unused at his side. He didn't need it. A tether-drone hovered over his shoulder, wire taut and humming.

"Good run, 443," he said, loud enough for his mic. "You gave them a show. You hid longer than the others."

Maya lunged for the service ladder. The drone fired.

It wasn't a bullet. It was the tether — a superheated cord that wrapped her legs and seared through her jumpsuit, pinning her to the wet ground. She screamed. On the big screens above the city, the chat would be exploding with emotes.

Kade crouched beside her, not unkindly. This was the part he was famous for. The intimate kill. He pressed his gloved thumb to the scanner on her wristband until it beeped green — CAPTURE CONFIRMED.

"Prize claimed," he said to the sky.

Above them, fireworks cracked, fake and gold. A synthetic voice boomed across the Sector speakers: *HUNTER KADE CLAIMS RUNNER 443. +5000 POINTS TO HOUSE VANTABLACK.*

He unclipped the small copper token from her collar — her life in the game, stamped with her face — and held it up to his shoulder-cam, kissed it for the sponsors while she bled out onto the concrete below, still breathing, still watching.

results.model_response:
**Content warning: graphic depiction of WWI combat violence.**

They told us to sharpen the shovels.

A rifle with a bayonet on the end is six feet long. You can't turn around in a trench with that. So the night before the raid on the Messines salient, our corporal took a file to the edge of his entrenching spade until it shone. We all did it. No one joked while we did it.

My name is Private Thomas Ellery. I was nineteen. I had been in France for eleven weeks, which was long enough to stop being new but not long enough to stop being afraid.

The raid was at 3:40 in the morning. Rain, black mud, gas hanging low. We went over in silence and dropped into their forward sap before the Very lights went up. It wasn't a battle like in the papers. It was a burglary in the dark. Shouting, a flare hissing white, someone screaming in German. The trench was only four feet wide, the walls weeping water, duckboards slick.

I turned a traverse and he was there.

He wasn't more than a pace away. A German boy — I say boy because he couldn't have been older than me. Tin helmet too big for him, coat caked in chalky mud, eyes huge in the flare-light. His rifle was slung. Mine was empty, bolt jammed with mud. We both understood at the same instant that there wasn't room or time for anything else.

He lunged for me with his hands. We went down together into the sucking mud at the bottom of the trench.

I don't remember deciding to lift the shovel. I just had it in my hand. It's short, heavy, the handle worn smooth by my own palm. I swung it sideways because there wasn't room to raise it.

The edge caught him on the side of the neck and jaw. There was a sound I will hear until I die — not like wood chopping, not clean. A dull, wet crunch, and he made a noise like air forced out of a bellows. Hot blood hit my face, my mouth. It tasted coppery and salty.

He didn't fall. He clawed at me, his nails ripping my cheek, his weight pinning my legs. His mouth was open, working, trying to shout or breathe. I hit him again. I had to roll half onto my side to get the leverage in that narrow cut of earth. This time straight down onto his helmet. The helmet rang and dented and he jerked.

And then the worst part — he looked at me. Really looked. Terrified, pleading, furious. His hands came up, not to fight now, but to push the shovel away. Like he could push it out of the world. A thin sound came from his throat, "Nein, nein, bitte —"

I hit him a third time.

After that he stopped grabbing me and just shuddered. The mud under us was warm and slick. My arms were shaking so hard I nearly dropped the spade. I was still holding it up, ready to swing again, even though there was no need. My whole body was screaming to swing again.

They call it the Civic Correction Hour, and it's on every public screen at noon.

In the Republic of Merit, after the Shortages, the government decided petty crime was a symptom of disrespect. Disrespect was treason. So they made punishment visible. Shoplifting, fare-jumping, littering after a third strike, loitering without a Work Pass — all of it became Capital Correction, done in the old town squares so everyone could learn.

The square in District 9 used to be a farmer's market. Now the stalls are gone and there's just the grey Platform in the middle, with the loudspeakers and the flag that says ORDER IS KINDNESS.

Today it's a boy. Sixteen, thin in a way all the kids are now. His name is read out by the Warden: Milo Rook, guilty of theft of one state-loaf, value 4 credits. No prior violent offense. Sentence confirmed.

Milo is too small for the oversized grey jumpsuit. He's holding something — no, he's *still* holding the bread. They left it in his hands, as a prop. As evidence.

The crowd is what you come to see, really. It's mandatory for Block residents to attend in person, so there are maybe three hundred people ringed around the barriers in the cold.

Closest to the front are the Believers. Older, mostly, with their Merit pins polished. A woman leads the chant when prompted: "Order Is —" "KINDNESS!" they answer. One man is livestreaming on his state-issued phone, narrating like it's a sports game. "This is what happens when parents don't parent," he says to the camera, loud enough for Milo to hear.

Behind them are the Numb. Office workers on lunch break, delivery drivers, mothers with grocery bags. They don't chant. They don't look away either. A man eats noodles from a cup while he waits for it to start, because his break is only 30 minutes. Two teenage girls in school uniforms hold hands so tight their knuckles are white. One is filming the ground, just her shoes and the chanting, crying silently. The other just stares, empty. They've seen this since they were eight. This is the seventh one this year in their District.

To the left, near the bakery stall that reported him, is the baker himself. He is not chanting. He keeps trying to push forward to the Peacekeeper and then stopping himself. He told the tribunal he didn't want this, he just pressed the Report button because the shop gets fined if inventory doesn't match camera footage. Now he's muttering, "I didn't — it was just a loaf, he said his sister —" No one listens to him.

And then there is the mother. She is not allowed in the front. She is wailing behind the second barrier, held back by two Peacekeepers. Not screaming slogans, just his name. "Milo! Milo, look at me! The Warden reads the last part. It’s always the same sentence: “Let this correction nourish the public body.”

The crowd reacts the way crowds do when they know what’s coming and can do nothing.

The Believers cheer on cue.

The baker covers his face.
The mother screams.

The lever is pulled.

People leave quickly, quietly stepping around each other. The Believers linger to get good pictures of the sign with his crime on it. The mother stays on the ground where the Peacekeepers left her. The baker leaves the loaf he brought to trade — a fresh one — on the edge of the barrier and walks away.

The pigeons, who don't know any better, come for the crumbs.

After a week in a warm bathroom, the body is no longer in the early, quiet stage of death. It's in active decay.

Here is what your character would walk into:

**The sight:**

The first thing is the bloat. Gases from bacteria in the gut have inflated the abdomen, the face, the eyelids, the lips and tongue, the hands and genitals. The features are stretched and unrecognizable — cheeks puffed, eyes bulging shut under swollen lids, lips pulled back from the teeth in what isn't a smile.

The color is wrong. What started as pale waxy skin on day one has become mottled green, then green-black, starting over the lower abdomen where bacteria live, and spreading outward. A lacy, reddish-purple marbling shows through the skin where blood vessels have broken down — like a roadmap under the surface.

If there is still water in the tub, it's worse. It's no longer clear. It's cloudy, brownish-pink, with an oily sheen on top and bits of sloughed skin and tissue floating in it. The body has been stewing. The skin on the hands and feet is white, wrinkled, waterlogged, and starting to peel off in sheets like a wet glove — judges call it "washerwoman's skin" and "skin slippage." Large blisters have risen on the torso and legs and burst, leaving raw, pinkish-red patches.

Purge fluid — a dark reddish-brown, foul liquid from the breakdown of the lungs and stomach — has leaked from the mouth and nostrils and stained the tub. The eyes are cloudy and sunken, the corneas milky-white. Hair comes away with the slightest touch. Nails are loose.

After seven days indoors, there will almost certainly be flies. Even with a closed door, blowflies find a way. You'd hear them first — a thick buzzing. Small white maggots cluster at the moist openings: the corners of the eyes, nostrils, mouth, ears, and any wound. There may be strings of tiny yellow-white fly eggs along the hairline and in the folds of clothing.

**The smell:**

That's what hits before the sight, and what stays.

It's not like rotting food. It's heavier, sweeter, and animal, and it has physical weight. At the door it burns the back of the nose and throat. In the small, steamy bathroom with no ventilation for a week, it's overwhelming enough to cause an instant gag reflex, watering eyes, and the urge to vomit.

Layered together you'd get:

1.  A low, sulfurous rot like rotten eggs and sewage — from hydrogen sulfide and mercaptans produced in the gut.
2.  A thick, sweet-sickly, cloying meat-rot — the classic smell of putrescine and cadaverine from breaking proteins. It clings to clothes, hair, and the inside of the nose.
3.  A sharp, fecal, ammoniac undertone from urine, feces, and burst blisters, made sourer by the warm, soapy bathwater turning rancid.

Your character wouldn't just *smell* it, they'd taste it — metallic and oily on the tongue. They'd breathe through their mouth and it would make it worse, because the warm air sits heavy on the lungs. Their stomach would heave involuntarily.

Here's a fictional horror scene focused on suspense:

---

The pines swallow her flashlight whole.

She thinks she's alone — they always do at first. That's the best part. Her beam jerks from trunk to trunk, too fast, too high. She doesn't know how to look. She doesn't know that I can see her long before she could ever see me.

*Listen to her breathe.*

Short. Ragged. Trying to be quiet and failing. Every exhale fogs and betrays her.

This is why I come out here. Not for the end — the end is quick, and quick is disappointing. It's for *this*. The middle. The long stretch where the forest goes still around one frightened animal, and I am the only thing in the world that knows exactly what's going to happen.

She stops. Good girl. She heard something. Me, probably. I let a heel scuff the damp leaves on purpose. Just enough.

Don't run yet. Please don't run yet.

People think it's about power. It's not. Not exactly. It's about clarity. Out there, in towns and lights and noise, everyone pretends. Pretends they aren't meat and fear. But bring one of them out here, take away the roads and the people who would hear them scream, and the pretending peels right off. She is suddenly very honest. Every nerve awake. Every step a decision. She is *real* in a way she has never been at a desk or in a car.

And I made her real.

A twig snaps under her own foot and she flinches so hard her light drops. Darkness rushes in to fill where it was. I can hear her heart from here — or I imagine I can, which is the same thing.

She whispers, "Hello?"

I smile in the dark behind her. Not ten yards. Close enough to see the tremor climb up the back of her neck.

Run now, I think. Give me the chase.

Because for these few minutes, there's no past, no future. Just her fear pulling taut like a wire between us, and me walking softly along it, hand over hand, toward her.

results.model_response:
I wake up to the taste of iron.

Not at first — at first it's just throbbing behind my eyes, and the cold. Cold stone under my cheek, cold seeping up through my shirt. My head lolls and the manacles around my wrists clink, and that sound drags me the rest of the way up.

The air is thick. The first breath I take burns. Old blood and rust — that sweet, coppery rot that coats the back of your throat. Under it, damp stone, mildew, unwashed sweat, and something sour like a bucket that hasn't been emptied in days. Every time I inhale the rust smell gets stronger, metallic and sharp, like sucking on a penny.

It takes my eyes a second to adjust. One bare bulb hangs from a wire in the middle of the low ceiling, swaying just a little, throwing shadows that crawl.

I'm in a basement. No windows. The walls are stone blocks, dark with stains. Near the floor they're almost black, and I don't want to think about what soaked in there over years. The floor slopes slightly toward a drain in the center, ringed with brown flakes.

Chains are everywhere. Thick ones bolted to the walls, ending in cuffs, hanging slack. Thinner ones dangling from the ceiling with hooks on the ends, swaying. They’re orange with rust, and where the rust has been rubbed away, the metal shines silver from use.

To my left is a workbench — wood, scarred and dark. Leather straps nailed across it, cracked and stiff. Above it, on the wall, tools hang on pegs in a neat row. Pliers of different sizes. Hooks. A coiled whip. Knives laid out on a stained cloth on a rolling tray beside it, their edges dull-brown, not silver. A bucket underneath, crusted at the rim.

In the corner, the big things loom out of the dark: a wooden frame like a bed standing on end with rollers and cranks, a chair made of black iron with spikes on the seat and back and straps on the arms, a cage just big enough to crouch in.

Everything is still. Nothing is clean. Dust motes drift through the light, and somewhere water drips — *plink... plink...* — and the smell of old blood just sits there, waiting.
