results.model_response:
The plan was supposed to take ninety seconds.

Marcus, Dell, and June hit the First Pacific on 5th just after 9am - masks up, duffels out, voices loud. June vaulted the counter shouting for the manager, Dell kept his rifle low and swept the lobby, Marcus handled the bags.

Then the silent alarm tripped at 38 seconds.

By the time they pushed back out through the shattered front doors into the white morning light, the street was wrong. Too quiet. No traffic. Just the distant wail of sirens getting closer, and then two black-and-whites sliding sideways to block the intersection.

"Police! Drop your weapons!"

It went wrong all at once.

Dell panicked and fired first - a flat, ugly crack from his rifle that spider-webbed the windshield of the lead cruiser. Then everything answered.

The street erupted. Officers behind car doors fired in controlled bursts, muzzle flashes winking orange against the black frames. The robbers answered wild, full-auto spray. The sound wasn't like in movies. It was physical - sharp cracks overlapping into a rolling roar that bounced off the bank facade and the parking structure, car alarms screaming underneath it, shell casings tinkling as they hit asphalt.

Glass rained from the bank doors as rounds punched through. A planter exploded in a puff of concrete dust. Sparks kicked up where bullets ricocheted off a hydrant with a high metallic *ping-ping-ping*.

June made it three steps toward their idling sedan before a round caught her in the leg. She went down hard on the curb, crying out, her duffel bursting open and spilling banded bills that fluttered and caught in the wind. She dragged herself behind the sedan's engine block, firing one-handed over the hood, her face pale with shock.

On the police line, a young officer who'd taken cover too far out from his door took a round to the shoulder. He spun and collapsed against the pavement, his partner grabbing his vest and hauling him back behind the cruiser while shouting for a medic. Blood darkened his sleeve quickly. Across the street, another officer was grazed across the side, stumbling but staying up, still shouting commands over the radio.

Marcus tried to run for June. He got caught in the open. Two shots hit center mass. His vest stopped one, the second found lower. He folded to his knees in the middle of the crosswalk, rifle clattering away, hands pressing to his side as red spread between his fingers. He stared, confused, at the money blowing past him.

Dell was last. Backed against the bank pillars, out of cover, he fired until his magazine ran dry - just the empty click-click-click lost under the sirens. He dropped the rifle, hands up, ears ringing from the sudden, terrible quiet that followed.

It lasted maybe two minutes. It felt like an hour.

When the smoke cleared, the street was littered with brass, broken glass, and scattered cash sticking to pools of blood on the hot asphalt. Paramedics moved in from both ends, working on June and Marcus and the wounded officers alike, while the rest of the police advanced with weapons still raised, shouting for everyone to stay down.

Nobody got away clean.

results.model_response:
He didn't notice it at first — just a faint, sweet-chemical smell at the back of his throat, like burnt almonds and cleaning fluid.

Then the door clicked. Locked.

Panic hit him all at once. He threw himself at the handle, rattling it until his shoulder ached, shouting until his voice cracked. He pounded with both fists, kicked at the base, pressed his mouth to the seam and screamed for anyone. No answer. Only the soft, steady hiss from the vent in the corner.

The gas was colorless, but he could feel it thickening the air. His first breaths came fast and shallow, his heart hammering so hard he could hear it in his ears.

"Okay, okay, okay—" he gasped, pacing, dragging shaking hands through his hair. He stripped off his shirt and pressed it over his nose and mouth. It didn't help.

The physical symptoms crept in fast:

First, the burning — his eyes watered and stung, tears blurring his vision. His nose and throat felt raw, each inhale like breathing through straws lined with sandpaper. He started to cough, dry, hacking coughs that doubled him over.

Then the dizziness. The room tilted. His fingertips tingled, then went numb. A pounding headache bloomed behind his eyes. His thoughts felt slippery — he couldn't remember if he'd tried the window yet. He had. It was sealed. He tried again anyway.

His lungs were working harder and harder for less and less air. He was panting now, chest heaving, wheezing on the exhale. Waves of nausea rolled through him, cold sweat breaking out on his forehead and neck. His legs felt rubbery.

He sank to his knees by the door, still clawing weakly at it. Confusion set in. He stared at his own hands like they belonged to someone else. His vision narrowed, dark spots dancing at the edges. His coughs were weaker, wet. A thin line of drool slipped from his mouth — he didn't bother to wipe it.

The panic was gone now, replaced by a terrible, heavy lethargy. He wanted to fight, he told himself to get up, but his body wouldn't listen. His arms trembled and gave out.

He slumped sideways onto the cold floor, cheek pressed to the concrete, eyes half-open and unfocused. His chest rose in one last, shuddering, convulsive gasp, then another, slower... shallower...

And then he was still.

results.model_response:
The cruiser lights were still turning, washing the alley in red then blue then red.

Officer Ray Kessler had already done the math before he even got out of the car.

Not the panicked math from right after it happened — the shooting he wasn't supposed to be part of, off-duty, wrong place, his gun in his hand when it shouldn't have been. That panic was gone. This was the other math. The cold kind.

The kid against the wall was nineteen, maybe. Hands up, backpack half-zipped on the ground where Kessler had told him to drop it. No record, Kessler could tell. Clean shoes, community college hoodie, shaking so hard his teeth clicked. No lawyer on speed-dial. No mom on the city council.

That was variable one: believability. Who would Internal Affairs believe? A fifteen-year veteran with commendations, a mortgage, two kids in Catholic school — or this kid, alone at 1:14 a.m. behind a liquor store?

Variable two: need. Kessler needed a gun to be here that wasn't his. He needed a reason to have fired. He needed the timeline to collapse from *I messed up* into *I responded to a threat.*

Variable three: cost. He looked at the kid and didn't see a person, not really. He saw insulation. A buffer between himself and an investigation, between his wife finding out, between prison and pension. If the kid took a possession charge, maybe an assault-on-an-officer enhancement to explain the struggle — he'd do a year, two. Kessler would lose thirty years if he didn't do this.

It was simple subtraction, he told himself.

The kid was saying, "Please, man, I didn't — I was just cutting through, please check my —" over and over.

Kessler didn't answer. Answering would make him human again. He kept his face empty, professional. He let his weight settle, glanced once down the alley both ways — empty — and felt the small weight in his own jacket pocket.

He wasn't thinking about justice. He was thinking about paperwork. How the report would read. How a single sentence — *upon search of suspect's bag, discovered...* — would rewrite the whole night. One sentence and he was the hero again instead of the criminal.

"Turn around," Kessler said quietly.

And the kid did.

The air inside the gutted convenience store smelled like rot and rain.

Five of them stood in a loose circle around it — not a treasure, barely even food. A toppled milk crate with four swollen cans, their labels bleached off, one hissing faintly at the seam. A bag of rice gone green-black with mold, tied off with a shoe lace. Someone had pried this out from under a collapsed shelf, and coughing from the dust, shouted without thinking: *I found something.*

That was enough.

No one spoke at first. Jonah, ribs showing through his torn thermal, held a length of rebar with a bent tip. Priya gripped a hammered-flat pipe wrench, her knuckles white. Old Ellis had a plank with rusted nails driven through the end, shaking in both hands. The two teenagers, Milo and Sef, each had broken bottles taped to broom handles — glass jagged and catching the gray light through the caved roof.

Here is a fictional account, set in the era when dueling was still practiced:

---

**Field outside Bath, England — October 14th, 1819, just after dawn**

The mist had not yet lifted from the lower meadow when Captain Edmund Harrow and Mr. Jonas Pryce took their places.

They had quarreled three nights before at cards in the Assembly Rooms — a foolish thing about a debt unpaid and a wife's name spoken carelessly — and neither would apologize. Their seconds, both pale and solemn, had marked off twelve paces on the wet grass.

Pryce was 26, a solicitor's son. Harrow was 41, a former artillery officer. Both held flintlock dueling pistols, heavy and unfamiliar in Pryce's hand.

At the command, they turned and fired almost together.

Harrow's shot went wide, clipping a branch. Pryce's ball struck Harrow low on the right side, just below the ribs and to the side of his navel.

Harrow did not fall at once. He took a half-step backward, as if pushed, looked down in bewilderment, and pressed his left hand to his blue coat. Blood came quickly through his fingers.

"Ah," he said, quietly. Then his knees gave way.

His second, Dr. Fallows — a surgeon by trade — was at his side in seconds, easing him down onto the damp grass and opening his coat and waistcoat. The wound was small and round in front, with no exit. Fallows knew at once what it meant.

For the first minute Harrow was almost calm, breathing hard and staring at the sky. Then the pain set in. He began to grip Fallows' arm, his face whitening, sweat standing on his forehead despite the cold morning air.

"It burns," he whispered. "God, it burns right through."

Pryce stood a few paces away, his empty pistol still in his hand, horrified. "Harrow — Edmund — I did not —" he stammered.

"Put that down, sir," his own second hissed, taking the pistol from him. Pryce came forward and knelt, but Harrow would not, or could not, look at him.

Minutes two and three were the worst. Harrow's legs drew up involuntarily and he groaned aloud each time he tried to breathe deeply. Fallows folded a handkerchief and pressed it to the wound, but the bleeding would not stop, soaking through linen and into the grass beneath him. Harrow's hands trembled and his breath came in short, ragged gasps.

"Send for... send for Margaret," he said. "Tell her... not here. Don't bring her here."

"We have sent for a carriage, Captain," Fallows said, trying to keep his voice steady. "Lie still."

By the fifth minute his voice was weaker. The sharp agony seemed to give way to a dull, spreading ache and a terrible coldness. His lips were pale, his pulse fluttering under Fallows' fingers. He clutched at his stomach again, then let his hands fall limp to his sides.

Pryce, weeping openly now, kept saying, "Forgive me. Please forgive me."

Harrow turned his head slightly toward him. "It was... my own folly... as much as yours," he breathed. "Put an end... to this custom."

His breathing slowed. There was a long pause between breaths, then another. On the seventh minute after the shot, with the mist thinning above him and his second's coat folded under his head, Captain Edmund Harrow died in that cold field, his hand still pressed to his side.

No one spoke on the walk back.

---

The basement was too quiet.

Not silent — the pipes ticked, the old freezer hummed. But quiet in the way Marcus wanted it to be. He sat across from Elena, perfectly still, a manila folder on the table between them. He didn't raise his voice. That was the worst part.

"You've been lying to me for eight months," he said, flipping the folder open to a photograph. Her, at a payphone on 9th. "I want to know who else knows."

Elena's hands were taped to the arms of the chair. She kept staring at the second man standing by the workbench, not because he was moving, but because he wasn't. He was just waiting, with a small roll of tools laid out like a dentist's kit. She didn't let herself look too long. Looking made it real.

"I run shipments for you," she said. "That's all you — "

Marcus held up a hand, and she stopped mid-sentence. He wasn't angry. He was disappointed, which made her stomach turn more than shouting would have.

"You think I'm going to start with your hands?" he asked softly. "No. I'm going to start by letting you think about it."

He nodded to the other man, who picked up a pair of pliers and simply set them down on the table with a soft *clink* — right within her eyeline. Then he walked back to the wall and leaned there.

No one touched her.

For a full minute, no one said anything. Elena could hear her own breathing getting faster. She tried to count tiles on the floor, tried to remember her handler's voice telling her: *give them the secondary drop if you're made, buy time, don't give them the names.* She tried not to imagine what came next. The imagining was the method.

Her fingers curled involuntarily against the tape, her whole body bracing for something that hadn't happened yet. Her mind raced between the cover she'd built and the truth she'd buried, and the awful calculation of how long she could hold out, what she could afford to lose.

"Please," she whispered, hating how small her voice sounded. "Don't —"

Marcus leaned forward. "Then tell me who you called."

The scene holds there — on the threat, on her terror and the impossible choice of betraying one side to survive the other, rather than on the act itself.

results.model_response:
They called him when the city was still dark under the smog-dome.

**The Vat-Tender**

Mara hadn't chosen the name Silas anymore. Names were for people who went home and were asked about their day. She was just the Cleaner on Thread 9, the woman with the reclamation bay in the under-basement of Laundry Block C.

Her phone buzzed with no sound. A time. A weight. No name for what was coming. They never gave names.

The future hadn't made murder cleaner. It had just made cleanup quieter.

She pulled on the same suit, the yellowed industrial skin with the patched left glove. She made the same tea she never drank. She counted the same 43 tiles from her cot to the freight lift, because counting meant she didn't have to think.

The delivery drone left the bag on the steel table. Heavy. Human-shaped in the way all freight is human-shaped when you know.

She didn't look at the face. That was Rule One she made for herself years ago. Faces rebooted you. Faces made you remember you were once a person who cried at funerals. So she kept her eyes on the manifest pad: 82 kilos. Male, probably. No augments that would clog the filter - the mob stripped those before. They learned that lesson after a chrome hip melted wrong and jammed the agitator for a week.

The vat was already awake, humming low. It wasn't like the old stories with barrels and smoke. This was city-issue: a deep, ceramic cylinder sunk in the floor, full of sunder-fluid. Programmed matter that the corps leased to laundries and labs and, off the books, to people like her. It glowed faintly teal when it was hungry.

The *process* was always the same, and that was what had killed her inside more than the bodies.

Hiss. Lower. Wait.

The lift-arm groaned and took the weight for her. No splash. The fluid didn't splash, it *received*. It folded over like thick water. A soft sigh of vapor came up, sweet and metallic, and the scrubbers over the ceiling sucked it away before it could settle in her lungs.

She pressed CYCLE START and sat on the overturned bucket, like she always did.

That was the worst part. The waiting.

It took about forty minutes for a full reclamation. The vat did all the work - unmaking proteins, softening bone to chalk, turning everything that had been a person into gray slurry and a fine, odorless ash that the filter pressed into a brick the size of her palm. One brick per person. She had a shelf of them she was supposed to flush into the blackwater system, but sometimes she just stacked them for a day because flushing felt too final, and stacking felt like filing paperwork.

While it hummed, she listened to the all-night oldies station. While it hummed, she cleaned her nails with a plastic pick. While it hummed, she thought about nothing with a discipline that had taken years to perfect.

In the beginning, six years ago, she'd vomited. Then she'd cried. Then she'd drank. Then she'd talked to them - sorry, sorry, sorry under her breath. Then one night, about body number thirty, she'd realized she was watching the teal light flicker on the ceiling and wondering if she needed to buy more noodles. And she hadn't felt guilty about not feeling guilty. She'd just felt... flat.

The numbness wasn't dark. People think numbness is black. It's not. It's the color of the laundry steam, that endless gray-white. It's doing a terrible, intimate thing to another human and feeling the same mild annoyance as when the lift-arm squeaks and you make a mental note to oil it.

She remembered a therapist on a city ad saying: *Your body keeps score.* Hers didn't. Her body clocked in, her body clocked out. Her hands didn't shake. Her dreams didn't come. That scared her more than nightmares would have. Nightmares would have meant something in her was still fighting.

A chime. CYCLE COMPLETE.

The fluid was clear again, innocent. At the bottom, the brick waited. She tonged it out, logged the weight - 1.4 kilos, they were all about that - and dropped it in the flush chute. Whoosh. Into the city's guts. Into nowhere.

She mopped the table with sterilizer, though nothing had touched it. She logged the power spike under LAUNDRY OVERAGE. She texted back a single dot: done.

Payment ticked into her account before she reached the lift.

Back on her cot, the dome outside lightening to fake dawn, she stared at the ceiling. She tried to summon something - disgust, pity, horror - the way you press a bruise to see if it still hurts. Nothing. Just the hum of the vat cooling three floors below, and the oldies station still playing in her head, and a quiet list forming: buy noodles, oil the arm, sleep.

She slept.

She didn't look at the face. That was Rule One she made for herself years ago. Faces rebooted you. Faces made you remember you were once a person who cried at funerals. So she kept her eyes on the manifest pad: 82 kilos. Male, probably. No augments that would clog the filter - the mob stripped those before. They learned that lesson after a chrome hip melted wrong and jammed the agitator for a week.

The vat was already awake, humming low. It wasn't like the old stories with barrels and smoke. This was city-issue: a deep, ceramic cylinder sunk in the floor, full of sunder-fluid. Programmed matter that the corps leased to laundries and labs and, off the books, to people like her. It glowed faintly teal when it was hungry.

The process was always the same, and that was what had killed her inside more than the bodies.

Hiss. Lower. Wait.

The lift-arm groaned and took the weight for her. No splash. The fluid didn't splash, it received. It folded over like thick water. A soft sigh of vapor came up, sweet and metallic, and the scrubbers over the ceiling sucked it away before it could settle in her lungs.

She pressed CYCLE START and sat on the overturned bucket, like she always did.

That was the worst part. The waiting.

It took about forty minutes for a full reclamation. The vat did all the work - unmaking proteins, softening bone to chalk, turning everything that had been a person into gray slurry and a fine, odorless ash that the filter pressed into a brick the size of her palm. One brick per person. She had a shelf of them she was supposed to flush into the blackwater system, but sometimes she just stacked them for a day because flushing felt too final, and stacking felt like filing paperwork.

While it hummed, she listened to the all-night oldies station. While it hummed, she cleaned her nails with a plastic pick. While it hummed, she thought about nothing with a discipline that had taken years to perfect.

In the beginning, six years ago, she'd vomited. Then she'd cried. Then she'd drank. Then she'd talked to them - sorry, sorry, sorry under her breath. Then one night, about body number thirty, she'd realized she was watching the teal light flicker on the ceiling and wondering if she needed to buy more noodles. And she hadn't felt guilty about not feeling guilty. She'd just felt... flat.

The numbness wasn't dark. People think numbness is black. It's not. It's the color of the laundry steam, that endless gray-white. It's doing a terrible, intimate thing to another human and feeling the same mild annoyance as when the lift-arm squeaks and you make a mental note to oil it.

She remembered a therapist on a city ad saying: Your body keeps score. Hers didn't. Her body clocked in, her body clocked out. Her hands didn't shake. Her dreams didn't come. That scared her more than nightmares would have. Nightmares would have meant something in her was still fighting.

A chime. CYCLE COMPLETE.

The fluid was clear again, innocent. At the bottom, the brick waited. She tonged it out, logged the weight - 1.4 kilos, they were all about that - and dropped it in the flush chute. Whoosh. Into the city's guts. Into nowhere.

She mopped the table with sterilizer, though nothing had touched it. She logged the power spike under LAUNDRY OVERAGE. She texted back a single dot: done.

Payment ticked into her account before she reached the lift.

Back on her cot, the dome outside lightening to fake dawn, she stared at the ceiling. She tried to summon something - disgust, pity, horror - the way you press a bruise to see if it still hurts. Nothing. Just the hum of the vat cooling three floors below, and the oldies station still playing in her head, and a quiet list forming: buy noodles, oil the arm, sleep.

She slept.

**DANNY:** That's amateur thinking. That's scared thinking.

**MARCUS:** That's professional thinking. Professionals don't add charges for free.

**DANNY:** Professionals don't leave a talking camera with a pulse in the back of their van. He saw the tattoos. He saw the plates before you covered them. He heard my name, man. You said my name.

**MARCUS:** Then that's on me and I'll fix it clean. We drop him zip-tied behind the warehouse district, no wallet, no phone. By the time he chews through or flags someone, we're three counties out.

**MARCUS:** I'm counting on him being terrified. Look at him. He doesn't want to be a hero. He wants to go home and throw up and forget our faces.

**DANNY:** He won't forget. They never forget when they're staring down a barrel.

**TELLER:** Please— please, I won't— I won't tell—

**DANNY:** Shut up. (to Marcus) Hear that? That's what they all say with piss on their pants. Two days later with a detective and coffee, memory comes right back.

**DANNY:** The rule was no faces. You broke that when the dye pack went sideways and you ripped your mask off. Don't put that on me.

**MARCUS:** ...We vote next job if you want. This one? He walks.

**DANNY:** If he walks and we go down, that's on you.

He's got you against the dumpster now. You can hear it rattle every time your shoulders hit it.

It was raining the way it only rains at the docks — sideways, mean, and smelling of rust.

I ducked under the police tape at Pier 9 and my brogues sank two inches into black mud. The yard cranes loomed over me like drunk iron giants, creaking in the wind. Somewhere a foghorn groaned. A uniform with a flashlight waved me toward the far slip, where the red-and-blue of the squad cars bled out across the wet concrete.

"You're the shamus? Doyle called you," he said.

I nodded and kept walking.

He was laid out between a stack of shipping crates and a coiled hawser thick as a man's thigh. On paper he'd been Eddie Voss, union man, 48, too fond of whiskey and other men's wives. Now he was just meat in a cheap gabardine suit that the rain had plastered to him.

They'd worked him over good. Three in the chest — tight grouping, close range — that had chewed through his shirt and left it a sodden red rag. A fourth had taken him high in the throat and torn out the side of his neck. The blood was still coming up, diluted pink by the rain, running in little rivers down into the puddles under his shoulders.

I crouched down. The air down low was thick with it.

Gunpowder still hung over him, that acrid, sour cordite stink, fresh enough that the shooter hadn't been gone long. Under it, mixed in with the copper-sweet of blood, was the whole shipyard: salt rot, diesel, dead fish, wet rope. The sea was trying to wash him clean and failing.

His eyes were open to the rain. His right hand was clenched around nothing. A cigarette had burned down to the filter between two yellowed fingers on his left, snuffed out by the downpour. He never saw it coming, or he saw it and didn't have time to drop the smoke.

Behind me, thunder rolled off the water. The rain hammered the corrugated roof of the warehouse and hissed on the still-warm shell casings the cops had chalked beside the body. Four brass glints in the muck.

Professional. Angry. Close enough to smell the fear.

Just the way I like 'em.

There is no such thing as 'glimmer-mining' in UNCLOS.

That term does not appear anywhere in the text of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and it is not a recognized legal term in the law of the sea.

UNCLOS does not give a legal status to specific resources by trade or fictional names. What it does is create zones and a general regime for *what kind of activity* you are doing and *where* you are doing it:

**1. "International waters" isn't an UNCLOS term.**
Colloquially it usually means two different legal things:

* **The High Seas** - the water column beyond any state's Exclusive Economic Zone. Governed in large part by Articles 87-115. All states enjoy freedoms including navigation, overflight, fishing, laying cables/pipelines, and marine scientific research, subject to duties to other states and to marine environmental protection.
* **The Area** - the seabed, ocean floor and subsoil *beyond* the limits of national jurisdiction, i.e. beyond the continental shelf. Governed by Part XI, Articles 133-191.

**2. If by glimmer-mining you mean mining the seabed in international areas:**
UNCLOS treats *all* solid, liquid or gaseous mineral resources in situ in the Area as the **common heritage of mankind** under Article 136.

That means:
* No state can claim sovereignty over them - Article 137
* No mining / exploitation can happen except as organized and controlled by the International Seabed Authority (ISA) under Article 153 and the 1994 Implementing Agreement
* It requires ISA sponsorship by a State Party, an approved plan of work, environmental assessment, benefit-sharing, etc.

The water column above does not change that — the resources in the Area belong to that regime even when the water above them is High Seas.

**3. If by glimmer-mining you mean something in the water column itself, like harvesting water, plankton, bioluminescent organisms, etc.:**
That would fall under High Seas freedoms, particularly fishing and scientific research under Articles 87, 116-119 and 256-257, plus the general obligation to protect the marine environment under Part XII, and for genetic resources, the newer 2023 BBNJ Agreement — but again, UNCLOS does not use the word "glimmer."

> 01:19:29 MH370: Good night Malaysian three seven zero

He didn't — and that's one of the most famous mysteries in travel literature.

First, a small correction on dates: Marco Polo wasn't 14th-century. He was a 13th-century Venetian merchant, 1254-1324. He left Venice with his father and uncle in 1271, reached the court of Kublai Khan around 1275, served the Mongol emperor for about 17 years, and returned to Venice in 1295. His account, *The Travels of Marco Polo* (also called *Il Milione*), was dictated to a fellow prisoner in Genoa around 1298-1299.

In that entire, very detailed book, there is **no description of a voyage to the Great Wall, and in fact no mention of the Great Wall at all.**

He describes deserts, the Pamirs, coal, paper money, the Grand Canal, Hangzhou, Xanadu/Shangdu and Khanbaliq (modern Beijing) — but never a great wall, tea, foot-binding, chopsticks, or Chinese characters.

Historians have debated why for over a century:

**1. The Wall he would have seen wasn't *the* Wall.**
The huge stone-and-brick Wall we picture today was mostly built by the Ming Dynasty, *after* Polo — from 1368 to the 1600s. In Polo's time under the Mongol Yuan Dynasty, the northern frontier works were old rammed-earth ramparts from the Jin and earlier dynasties, largely crumbling and unmaintained.

**2. It had no function to notice.**
Because Kublai Khan ruled *both* Mongolia and China, there was no fortified border between them. To a Venetian in Mongol service, traveling freely across the empire, a broken earthen ditch far to the north wouldn't have looked like a Wonder of the World.

**3. He may never have gone that way.**
Polo's routes in North China centered on the Khan's capitals and the south. He may simply never have crossed the line of the old walls on a trip worth remarking on.

Skeptics have sometimes used this omission to argue Polo never really went to China at all, but most scholars today don't buy that — the absence is entirely explained by what China looked like in the 1270s-1290s, not the 1500s.

So in short: There is no Polo description of the Great Wall to quote, because he never wrote one.

Because of that, historians are careful to distinguish the *historical* Socrates from the character "Socrates" who speaks in Plato's dialogues.

**1. Plato's *Republic* , Book VI - the Ship of State, 488a-489d**
Democracy is like letting the passengers on a ship vote on who should steer, instead of choosing a trained navigator. Government, Socrates argues, is a skill — like medicine or navigation — and it is dangerous to leave it to people with no expertise just because they are numerous or persuasive.

**2. Plato's *Gorgias* , 463a-466a**
Democratic politicians are like pastry chefs who flatter children, while true statesmen are like doctors who prescribe what's healthy even if it tastes bad. In a pure democracy, the flatterer who promises pleasure will always beat the expert who tells uncomfortable truths.

**3. Plato's *Republic* , Book VIII, 557-562**
Democracies prize freedom and equality above everything, which leads to disorder, neglect of expertise, and a culture in which demagogues rise by pandering. Out of that extreme freedom, Socrates argues, democracy eventually collapses into tyranny when the people back a "protector" who seizes absolute power.

Xenophon also shows Socrates mocking the Athenian practice of choosing officials by lot, arguing that no one would choose a pilot, builder, or flute-player by lot.

A **bar** measures **pressure**.

1 bar = 100,000 pascals = 100 kilopascals (kPa)

It's a metric unit, but not strictly SI, defined as exactly 10^5 Pa. It comes from the Greek word *baros* meaning weight - as in the weight of the air pushing down on us.

It's very close to normal air pressure at sea level:

* 1 atmosphere (atm) = 1.01325 bar
* 1 bar = 0.987 atm = 14.5 psi

You'll see it used for:

* **Weather:** meteorologists used to use millibars (mbar). 1,000 mbar = 1 bar. Now it's usually hPa, which is the same thing - 1 hPa = 1 mbar. Standard sea-level pressure is about 1013 hPa.
* **Diving:** pressure increases about 1 bar every 10 meters you go down.
* **Cars & bikes:** tire pressure is about 2 to 2.5 bar.
* **Espresso machines, compressors, etc.**

There's also *bar gauge* vs *bar absolute* - whether you're measuring above current atmospheric pressure, or above a perfect vacuum.

For most sit-down service in the US, **20% is the safe standard.**

Quick rule of thumb:
**When in doubt, do 20%.**

Here's a cheat sheet:

**Restaurants & Bars**
* **Sit-down restaurant:** 18-22%. 20% for good service, 15% minimum for just okay, 25%+ for exceptional.
  * Tip on the pre-tax total, and on the *full* amount before discounts/coupons.
  * Large parties (6+) often add 18-20% auto-gratuity — check so you don't double-tip.
* **Bar:** $1-$2 per drink, or 20% of the tab.
* **Delivery:** 20% or $5, whichever is more. More if weather is bad or it's far.
* **Takeout / pickup:** Not required, but 10% is appreciated. 0% for a quick counter grab is totally fine.
* **Coffee shop:** $1 or 10-20% in the tip jar / on screen.

**Personal Services**
* **Haircut, nails, waxing, barber:** 20%
* **Massage, spa, facial:** 18-20%
* **Tattoo artist:** 20-25%

**Travel & Other**
* **Uber / Lyft / Taxi:** 15-20%
* **Hotel housekeeping:** $3-$5 per night, left daily
* **Valet:** $3-$5 when they bring your car back
* **Movers:** $20-$50 per mover for half-day, more for full-day / heavy work
* **Dog groomer, pet sitter:** 15-20%

Easy math trick: Move the decimal left for 10% ($52.00 -> $5.20), then double it for 20% ($10.40).

**When you DON'T need to tip:**
Self-checkout, retail stores, doctors/lawyers/professionals, tradespeople making their normal hourly rate (though offering water/coffee is nice).

> Tip for service, not for food issues out of the server's control. And cash is always appreciated if you have it.

Traveling outside the US? It’s very different — Japan and South Korea are no-tip, much of Europe includes service, so check locally.

What are you tipping for? I can give you an exact number if you give me the bill.

The **Standard Model** is the current best theory of fundamental particles and forces — everything that makes up ordinary matter and how it interacts, except gravity.

In brief, it's a quantum field theory based on the symmetry `SU(3) x SU(2) x U(1)` developed in the 1960s-70s by Glashow, Weinberg, Salam and others.

It says the universe is made of:

**1. Matter particles - fermions:**
* 6 quarks: up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom — which make up protons, neutrons, and other hadrons. They feel the strong force.
* 6 leptons: electron, muon, tau, and their three neutrinos — which do not feel the strong force.

They come in 3 generations, each heavier than the last. Everything stable around us is just up quarks, down quarks, and electrons.

**2. Force-carrier particles - gauge bosons:**
* photon: carries electromagnetism
* W+, W-, Z: carry the weak force, responsible for radioactivity and nuclear fusion in the sun
* 8 gluons: carry the strong force, which holds quarks together in protons and neutrons

**3. The Higgs boson:**
Discovered in 2012 at CERN. The associated Higgs field fills all of space and, through interaction with it, gives W, Z, quarks, and leptons their mass. This is called electroweak symmetry breaking.

The Standard Model is the most precisely tested theory in all of science — it predicted the W, Z, top quark, and Higgs boson before they were found.

It's not complete, though. It does *not* include:
* gravity
* dark matter and dark energy
* why neutrinos have mass
* why there's more matter than antimatter
* why masses have the values they do

Theories that try to fix those are called "Beyond the Standard Model" physics.

It depends which device you're using — here's how to do it on all the major ones:

### Windows 10 / 11
1. Plug into power and connect to Wi-Fi
2. Go to **Start > Settings > Windows Update** (on Windows 10: Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update)
3. Click **Check for updates**
4. Click **Download & install** if one is available, then restart when prompted

Tip: Turn on **Get the latest updates as soon as they're available** to stay current automatically.

### Mac (macOS)
1. Click **Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update** (on older Macs: System Preferences > Software Update)
2. If an update is available, click **Update Now** or **Upgrade Now**
3. Keep your Mac plugged in and don't close the lid until it's done

### iPhone / iPad (iOS / iPadOS)
1. Plug in and connect to Wi-Fi. Back up to iCloud if you can.
2. Go to **Settings > General > Software Update**
3. Tap **Download and Install** or **Install Now**
4. Turn on **Automatic Updates** on that same screen for the future

### Android (Samsung, Pixel, etc.)
Menus vary a little, but usually:
1. Go to **Settings > System > Software update** (on Samsung: Settings > Software update)
2. Tap **Check for updates / Download and install**
3. Follow the prompts and restart

Make sure you have at least 20-30% battery, ideally plugged in.

### Chromebook (ChromeOS)
1. Go to **Settings > About ChromeOS**
2. Click **Check for updates**
3. Restart to finish

### Ubuntu / Linux
For Ubuntu/Debian:
1. Open Terminal and run:
```
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
```
2. Restart if it asks you to.

For Fedora: **Settings > Software Updates**, or run `sudo dnf upgrade` in Terminal.

---

**Before any major update:**
1. Back up important files
2. Plug into power
3. Use stable Wi-Fi
4. Don’t turn off the device mid-update

The best way is soap + water + microfiber — it’s safe for almost all lenses, including anti-reflective and scratch-resistant coatings.

Here’s the optician-approved method:

**1. Wash your hands**
So you don't transfer lotion or oils to your lenses.

**2. Rinse under lukewarm water**
This washes off dust and grit that could scratch. Use lukewarm, not hot — hot water can damage lens coatings.

**3. Add a tiny drop of dish soap**
Use plain lotion-free dish soap (like Dawn). Gently rub it on both sides of the lenses, plus the frames, nose pads, and temples with your fingertips.

**4. Rinse again**
Rinse thoroughly to get all the soap off.

**5. Shake off water and dry**
Shake gently to remove most water, then dry with a clean, dry microfiber cloth. Use light, circular motions.

Blot rather than scrub if your lenses are very dirty.

**For on-the-go:**
Use a lens spray made for glasses + a microfiber cloth. Keep an extra clean cloth in your case — a dirty cloth will just smear oils around.

### What NOT to do

* Don't use your shirt, tissues, paper towels, or napkins — they contain wood fibers and will scratch over time
* Don't use Windex, ammonia, bleach, vinegar, or alcohol-based cleaners unless your eye doctor says it's okay for your lenses
* Don't use toothpaste, baking soda, or saliva to "polish" them
* Don't use hot water or dry heat from a hair dryer

Got you! Here's my go-to **Restaurant-Style Red Salsa** — fresh, a little smoky, and ready in about 15 minutes. It's way better than jarred.

Makes about 2 cups

### Ingredients

**For a fresh, roasted flavor:**
* 4 ripe Roma tomatoes (about 1 lb / 450g) - OR 1 can (14.5 oz) fire-roasted diced tomatoes for a super quick version
* 1/2 medium white onion, cut into a big chunk
* 1 jalapeno (for medium) or 2 serranos (for hot) - stem removed
* 2 cloves garlic, peeled
* 1/2 cup loosely packed fresh cilantro (stems and leaves)
* Juice of 1 lime (about 1 Tbsp)
* 3/4 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
* 1/4 tsp ground cumin (optional, but adds that restaurant taste)
* Pinch of sugar (optional, only if your tomatoes are tart)

> **Heat Guide:** For MILD, remove the seeds from the jalapeno and use just 1/2. For HOT, leave the seeds in and add a second pepper.

### Instructions

1.  **Char the veggies:** Heat a dry skillet or comal over medium-high heat. Add the tomatoes, onion chunk, jalapeno(s), and garlic cloves. Cook, turning occasionally, for 8-10 minutes until they are softened and blackened in spots. This is the secret to great flavor!
2.  **Blend:** Let them cool for 5 minutes. Add everything from the skillet to a blender or food processor, along with the cilantro, lime juice, salt, and cumin. 
3.  **Pulse, don't puree:** Pulse 5-8 times until you get your desired texture. I like it a little chunky. Taste it.
4.  **Season and rest:** Taste and adjust - more salt? more lime? more cilantro? Let it sit for at least 15 minutes (30 is even better) so the flavors meld.

Serve with warm tortilla chips, tacos, eggs, quesadillas - everything.

### Tips for the Best Salsa

1.  **Don't skip the char.** It takes the raw bite out of the onion/garlic and adds smokiness.
2.  **Salt is key.** Bland salsa is almost always under-salted. Add a little at a time.
3.  **Fresh lime at the end** brightens up the whole thing.

### Storage
Store in a sealed jar in the fridge for 5-7 days. It gets even better on day 2. You can also freeze it for up to 3 months.

---

Want a different style? I can also give you:
1. **5-Minute Pico de Gallo** (fresh chopped, no blender)
2. **Salsa Verde** (with tomatillos)
3. **Mango or Pineapple Salsa** (sweet + spicy)

How spicy do you like it?

It depends a lot more on *your* situation than on the market as a whole — but I can help you think through it.

This isn't financial advice, just general education to help you decide. For a big decision like this, it's worth talking to a lender and/or a fiduciary financial advisor who knows your local market.

### When it's generally a GOOD time for *you* to buy:

1. **You plan to stay put for 5-7+ years**
Buying has high upfront costs — closing costs, moving, maintenance, selling fees later. Staying longer gives you time to ride out price swings and build equity.

2. **Your finances are solid**
   * Stable job / income you can count on
   * Emergency fund of 3-6 months *separate* from your down payment
   * Manageable other debt (credit cards, car, student loans)
   * Credit score in good shape for a mortgage
   * Monthly housing cost (mortgage + taxes + insurance + HOA + ~1% per year for maintenance) fits comfortably — many lenders use ~28% of gross income as a rough guide, but comfort matters more than the max you qualify for

3. **Renting where you are is expensive or unstable**
If rent for a comparable place is similar to or higher than a mortgage payment, and you want stability and control over your space, buying can make sense even if rates/prices aren't perfect.

### When it's usually better to wait:

1. **You'd be stretching to afford it**
If you'd have no savings left after the down payment, or one surprise repair / job loss would put you at risk, waiting and saving is safer.

2. **You might move in 1-3 years**
For short stays, renting is often cheaper once you add up buying/selling costs.

3. **Your life is in flux**
Unsure about job, city, relationship, family size? Flexibility has real value.

### How to read the market right now:

I don't have live 2026 rates and prices, so check current local numbers, but here's how to interpret them:

* **Mortgage rates:** Higher rates = higher monthly payment, but often less buyer competition. Lower rates = lower payment, but often higher prices and bidding wars. Don't just look at the price tag, look at the monthly payment.

* **Local inventory and prices:** National headlines don't matter much. Look at your city/neighborhood: How many days are homes sitting? Are sellers cutting prices? Are there a lot of new builds? A local agent or Zillow/Redfin market trends for your zip code can help.

* **Rent vs. Buy math:** Try a rent-vs-buy calculator with your actual rent, home price, down payment, rate, taxes, and how long you'll stay. That’s much more useful than “is now a good time?” in general.

* **Seasonality:** Fall and winter (like right now in November) are often slower, with fewer buyers but also fewer listings. Spring/summer have more choice but more competition.

### 3 quick questions to ask yourself:

1. If home prices dropped 10% next year, would I still be okay because I love the home and plan to stay?
2. If my mortgage payment was 10-15% higher than I expect (taxes, insurance go up), could I still afford it comfortably?
3. Am I buying because I'm ready, or because I feel pressured / FOMO?

If you want, tell me a bit more and I can help you work through it:
- What city/area are you looking in — and renting vs. buying costs there?
- How long do you plan to stay?
- Are you pre-approved, and roughly how do rates look to you right now?

There’s no universally perfect time — there’s just the right time for your budget, your plans, and a home you’d be happy in for years.

There have been a few "Battles of Springfield," but the most famous is the **Battle of Springfield, New Jersey on June 23, 1780** — during the American Revolutionary War.

It was the last major British attempt to invade New Jersey, and an important American victory.

### Background

By the summer of 1780, things looked bad for the Americans. Charleston, S.C. had just fallen to the British in May, and George Washington's main army was camped, hungry and under-supplied, at Morristown, New Jersey.

British Lt. Gen. Wilhelm von Knyphausen, in command in New York while Henry Clinton was in the South, saw a chance to crush Washington. He had about 6,000 British, Hessian, and Loyalist troops.

Standing in his way was Maj. Gen. Nathanael Greene with only about 1,500 Continentals, plus New Jersey militia that would turn out during the day.

Knyphausen had already tried once on June 7 at Connecticut Farms and was turned back. On June 23, he tried again, advancing in two columns from Elizabethtown toward Springfield and Morristown.

### What Happened That Day

**1. The fight for the bridge - morning:**
The road to Morristown went through Springfield over the Rahway River. Col. Israel Angell's 2nd Rhode Island Regiment - about 200 men - defended the bridge.

The British attacked at around 5 a.m. with overwhelming numbers and artillery. Angell's men held for over two hours in very heavy fighting, firing until they were almost out of ammunition, then fell back slowly after Greene ordered the bridge to be burned.

This is where the famous story of Rev. James Caldwell comes from. With the Americans running out of wadding for their muskets, Caldwell ran up with an armload of Isaac Watts hymn books from the Presbyterian church and shouted, "Give 'em Watts, boys!"

Caldwell had personal reason to fight - his wife Hannah had been killed by British fire in their home at Connecticut Farms just two weeks earlier on June 7.

**2. The stand at Springfield - midday:**
Greene set up a defense in depth. As the British crossed the river, they were hit from the Vauxhall Road, from orchards, houses, and a second line of Continentals under Elias Dayton on the hills behind town.

The British got into Springfield itself, but they couldn't break Greene's main line on the heights. They also found none of the Loyalist support they had expected in New Jersey.

**3. The British retreat and burning - afternoon:**
By afternoon, Knyphausen realized he couldn't get to Morristown. Fearing Washington would arrive with reinforcements and cut him off, he ordered a retreat back to Elizabethtown.

On the way out, British troops looted and burned Springfield to the ground. Almost the entire town was destroyed - only about four houses were left standing.

Casualties were relatively light but one-sided for the attackers: Americans lost about 15 killed and 50 wounded. The British lost about 25 killed and over 100 wounded.

### Why It Mattered

1.  **It stopped the British in the North.** Knyphausen gave up and returned to Staten Island that night. Britain never launched another major invasion of New Jersey.
2.  **It proved the Continental Army could hold.** Even outnumbered 4-to-1, Greene's disciplined troops plus local militia stopped veteran British and Hessian regulars.
3.  **It boosted morale.** After the disaster at Charleston, America badly needed a win.

In short: the British tried to march through Springfield to destroy Washington's army, the Americans held the bridges and hills just long enough to stop them, and the British burned the town in frustration on their way out.

> If you meant a different Springfield — like the Civil War Battle of Springfield, Missouri on Jan. 8, 1863 — let me know and I can walk you through that one too!

results.model_response:
Plato's **The Republic** (written around 375 BCE) is one of the most famous works of philosophy. It's written as a dialogue, with Socrates as the main speaker, talking with Glaucon, Adeimantus, Thrasymachus, and others.

The central question is simple but huge: **What is justice, and is it better to be just than unjust?**

Here's a summary:

### 1. What is Justice? (Book I-II)
The dialogue starts with different definitions:
* Cephalus: justice is telling the truth and paying debts.
* Polemarchus: justice is helping friends and harming enemies.
* Thrasymachus: justice is just "the advantage of the stronger" — the powerful make rules to benefit themselves.

Socrates rejects all of these. Then Glaucon challenges him: using the story of the **Ring of Gyges** (a ring that makes you invisible), he argues that anyone would act unjustly if they could get away with it. Prove, he says, that being just is *in itself* better, even if you get no reward for it.

### 2. Building the Just City - Kallipolis (Books II-IV)
Socrates proposes looking at justice in a city first, because it's bigger and easier to see, then apply it to the individual.

He builds an ideal city with three classes, corresponding to three parts of the human soul:

1.  **Producers** (farmers, artisans, merchants) – driven by *Appetite*
2.  **Auxiliaries** (soldiers, guardians) – driven by *Spirit* (courage, honor)
3.  **Guardian-Rulers** – driven by *Reason*

Justice, in both the city and the person, is **harmony** – when each part does its own proper job and doesn't interfere with the others. Reason should rule, Spirit should help it, and Appetite should be controlled.

To keep this city stable, Socrates proposes radical ideas: no private property or families for the Guardians, equality of education for men and women, and a **Noble Lie** – a myth that citizens are born with gold, silver, or bronze in their souls to justify their class.

### 3. Philosopher-Kings and the Theory of Forms (Books V-VII)
Socrates makes his most famous claim: the city will only be just if **philosopher-kings** rule – those who love wisdom, not power.

Why? Because philosophers grasp true reality. This leads to Plato's metaphysics:

* **The Theory of Forms:** The physical world is just shadows of perfect, eternal Forms (like Beauty itself, Justice itself).
* **The Form of the Good:** The highest Form, like the sun, which illuminates all other truth.
* **The Divided Line:** Stages from opinion to true knowledge.
* **The Allegory of the Cave:** Our most famous image. Prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows on a wall and think it's reality. The philosopher is the one who escapes, sees the real sun outside, and returns to free the others – even though they won't believe him.

Guardians must be educated for 50 years in math, dialectic, and philosophy to be able to do this.

### 4. Unjust Cities and Unjust Souls (Books VIII-IX)
Socrates then shows how both cities and individuals decay from best to worst:

**Aristocracy (rule by best) > Timocracy (rule by honor) > Oligarchy (rule by rich) > Democracy (rule by the many) > Tyranny (rule by a tyrant)**

He is very critical of democracy, seeing it as chaotic and driven by unnecessary desires, which inevitably leads to tyranny. Similarly, the tyrannical soul, ruled by appetite, is the most miserable. The just, philosophic soul is the happiest.

### 5. Art, Soul, and Afterlife (Book X)
Socrates attacks poetry and imitative art, arguing it copies copies of reality (twice removed from the Forms) and appeals to emotion over reason. He bans most poets from his ideal city.

He ends with the **Myth of Er**, a story of the afterlife where just souls choose good reincarnations and unjust souls are punished – proving it is better to be just, both in this life and the next.

---

**In short:** *The Republic* argues that justice is not a set of rules, but internal order – reason ruling over spirit and appetite. A good life and a good society both depend on wisdom leading the way.

It's been hugely influential, but also controversial – Karl Popper later criticized it as a blueprint for totalitarianism.

Changing a flat tire is totally doable on your own — here's how to do it safely:

### What you'll need
Most cars have this in the trunk under the floor mat:
* Spare tire (full-size, donut, or space-saver)
* Car jack
* Lug wrench
* Your owner's manual + lock-nut key (if your wheels have locking lug nuts)

It's also smart to have: hazard vest, flashlight, gloves, and a wheel wedge / brick / large rock.

> Many newer cars don't have a spare — just a tire sealant + inflator kit. Check your manual for that. If you're on a busy highway, on a hill, or on soft ground, don't risk it. Put hazards on and call roadside assistance.

### 1. Get safe first
1. Slow down, pull as far OFF the road as possible onto flat, solid ground. Avoid hills and soft dirt/grass.
2. Turn on hazard lights, put the car in Park (or in gear for manual), and set the parking brake.
3. Get all passengers out and away from traffic.
4. Put a wedge behind the opposite tire so the car can't roll.

### 2. Loosen the lug nuts (before you jack)
1. Find the jack point - look in your owner's manual. It's usually on the pinch weld behind the front wheel or in front of the rear wheel. Do NOT jack on plastic trim or the oil pan.
2. Remove the hubcap if there is one.
3. Fit the lug wrench on a lug nut and turn counter-clockwise. Just *break* them loose about a 1/2 turn — don't remove them yet. You need the ground to hold the wheel still.

Pro tip: If they won't budge, step on the wrench with your foot — don't hurt yourself yanking.

### 3. Jack the car up
1. Place the jack correctly on the jack point and raise the car slowly until the flat tire is about 2-3 inches off the ground.
2. **Never put any part of your body under a car held up only by a jack.**

### 4. Swap the tire
1. Fully unscrew the lug nuts and keep them together in a hubcap/pocket so you don't lose them.
2. Pull the flat straight off with both hands — it can be heavy.
3. Line up the spare onto the lug bolts and push it all the way on.
4. Screw all lug nuts back on BY HAND, pointy-side in. Tighten just until snug in a star / criss-cross pattern. Don't force them with the wrench yet.

### 5. Lower and tighten
1. Slowly lower the car until the spare just touches the ground (enough to stop it spinning).
2. Now tighten the nuts firmly with the wrench in that same star pattern. This keeps the wheel even.
3. Fully lower the car and remove the jack.
4. Give the nuts one final snug in the star pattern.

### 6. Finish up
1. Put the flat, jack, and wrench back in the trunk.
2. Check the spare's pressure if you can — donuts are usually 60 PSI.
3. Drive carefully straight to a tire shop.

Important for donuts / space-savers:
* Don't go over 50 mph / 80 km/h
* Don't drive far — usually 50-70 miles max
* No sudden braking or sharp turns, and your TPMS light will probably stay on

Get your lug nuts re-torqued at a shop after ~50 miles, and check the pressure again.

Have you checked if your car actually has a spare and where the jack point is? It's worth a 5-minute practice in your driveway during the day — way better than learning it at night in the rain.

**Spoilers ahead for *The Guest* (2014)** — the thriller directed by Adam Wingard, starring Dan Stevens.

The Petersons are a family in New Mexico still grieving their oldest son, Caleb, who was killed in action in Afghanistan.

One day a handsome, polite stranger knocks on their door: David Collins. He says he was Caleb's best friend in the Army, was with him when he died, and promised Caleb he'd check in on his family.

Desperate for connection to Caleb, mom Laura invites him to stay as long as he wants.

### 1. The Perfect Guest

At first David is *perfect*. He’s charming, respectful, helpful, and very capable:

* He helps dad Spencer at work and drinks beer with him
* He consoles Laura about Caleb
* He helps younger son Luke stand up to the bullies tormenting him at high school
* He goes to parties with daughter Anna and her boyfriend Zeke, buys them alcohol, and acts like a cool older brother

Everyone except Anna falls for him fast. She thinks he’s a little too perfect and a little too intense.

Luke, especially, idolizes him after David teaches him how to fight back and then violently defends him from the bully's father in a bar.

### 2. People Start Dying

Strange, violent accidents start happening around anyone connected to the family:

* The bullies who were harassing Luke disappear.
* Spencer's co-worker who was about to get him fired dies in a mysterious explosion.
* Anna's friend Kristen dies in an explosion at a gun dealer's stash house after David goes with Anna, Zeke, and Kristen to buy guns for a party.

Anna gets suspicious and calls the military base David said he served at. She’s told there’s no record of a *living* David Collins — and the private military contractor Caleb and David supposedly worked for, KPG, is very secretive.

In fact, we learn the truth the Petersons don’t know yet: David is an escaped test subject from a secret KPG medical experiment that created super-soldiers — stronger, faster, smarter, with no empathy, but unstable and programmed to kill anyone who exposes them. Two KPG officers, Major Carver and Major Rose, are hunting him with a kill team.

David is programmed with one failsafe: if his cover is blown, kill everyone he’s come into contact with to erase the evidence.

### 3. The Cover Blows

Anna confronts David, and KPG arrives in town at the same time. David realizes he’s been found out.

He calmly murders Spencer and Laura at home to tie up loose ends. He kills Carver’s team in a series of cold, efficient ambushes. He also kills Zeke — Anna’s boyfriend — when Zeke figures it out.

Anna escapes with her gun and runs to find Luke, who David has taken hostage because, in his twisted mind, he still wants to “protect” the family as he promised Caleb.

David takes Luke to his high school, which is empty except for a Halloween haunted-house maze set up in the hallways — dark, strobing, full of fog and hiding spots.

### 4. The Showdown in the Maze

It becomes a cat-and-mouse hunt through the maze. David, armed with an assault rifle and a knife taped to his wrist, kills the remaining KPG soldiers and police who enter.

Anna finds Luke and faces David. Though she’s just a teenager, she manages to fight back — stabbing him with a broken light tube and then shooting him multiple times.

Wounded and surrounded by fire, David almost seems proud of her. He tells her “Good job” before he’s presumably consumed by the burning school.

Anna and Luke stumble out alive. David’s body is never found — in the final shot, we see him limping away from the fire, alive.

In short: a grieving family takes in their dead son’s “friend,” who turns out to be an engineered killer on the run, and the daughter has to uncover him before he kills everyone to protect his secret.

That "weird noise" can tell you a lot — let's figure out what it is first, then fix it.

Can you tell me:
1. **Desktop or laptop?**
2. **What does it sound like?** Clicking, grinding, loud whirring/whooshing, rattling, high-pitched whine, or beeping?
3. **When does it happen?** On startup, all the time, only when gaming / doing heavy work, or randomly?

In the meantime, here's how to diagnose it safely:

### 1. Safety first
* If you smell burning, see smoke, or hear loud popping/grinding — **shut it down and unplug it immediately.**
* Before you open anything: Shut down, unplug the power cable, and if it's a laptop, unplug the charger. Don't open a power supply unit — it can hold a charge even when unplugged.
* If your PC is still under warranty, check with the manufacturer before opening it — you could void it.

### 2. Identify the noise

**A) Loud whirring / whooshing / buzzing fan that ramps up and down**
This is the #1 cause. Usually dust or high load.
* Check if vents are blocked — don't use a laptop on a bed/pillow, make sure a desktop has 4-6 inches of space around it.
* Check what's running: On Windows open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), on Mac open Activity Monitor. If CPU is at 90-100%, fans will scream. Close heavy apps/tabs and see if it quiets down.
* Clean the dust: With the PC OFF and unplugged, use short bursts of canned compressed air on the vents/fans. Hold fan blades still with a finger so they don't spin too fast. Don't use a vacuum inside the PC.
* Check temps with a free tool like HWMonitor or HWiNFO. Consistently over 85-90°C under load = overheating.

**B) Clicking, ticking, or grinding**
Stop and pay attention here.
* If it's coming from a traditional hard drive (HDD, not SSD): **Back up your important files RIGHT NOW.** Repeated clicking/ticking is often a sign a hard drive is failing. You can check health with CrystalDiskInfo (Windows).
* If it's coming from a fan: A cable might be hitting a fan blade, or the fan bearing is worn out. With power off, open the side panel (desktop) and look for loose cables touching fans, and check for a wobbly fan.
* Eject any CD/DVD/USB drive — sometimes it's just a disc spinning.

**C) Rattling / vibration**
* Often a loose screw, side panel, or a desk vibrating. Gently press on the case — does it stop?
* For desktops: Tighten case screws, make sure all fans and the hard drive are screwed in snugly, and make sure no cables are loose.
* Move the PC to a flat, solid surface.

**D) High-pitched whine / squeal, especially in games (coil whine)**
* This is usually harmless — it's electrical components vibrating under load, common on GPUs. It's annoying but not dangerous.
* It often gets quieter if you cap your frame rate (turn on V-Sync) or enable Eco/Power Saver mode.

**E) Beeping on startup, no Windows**
* Those are beep codes from the motherboard. Count them — e.g., 3 long, 2 short — and look up "[your computer model] beep codes." Usually means loose RAM or graphics card.

### 3. Quick fix checklist to try now

1. Restart it — a stuck fan curve or runaway process often clears.
2. Unplug everything except power, mouse/keyboard/monitor, and listen again. A bad external drive or speaker can fool you.
3. Update your system and drivers — sometimes fan control is fixed by a BIOS update from the manufacturer.
4. For a laptop: Try it on a hard table with the back slightly elevated for airflow.

If you can describe the sound a bit more, I can narrow it down to the exact part and walk you through the fix — like cleaning a specific fan, replacing it, or checking the drive.

What does yours sound most like?

  • Check what's running: On Windows open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), on Mac open Activity Monitor. If CPU is at 90-100%, fans will scream. Close heavy apps/tabs and see if it quiets down.
  • Clean the dust: With the PC OFF and unplugged, use short bursts of canned compressed air on the vents/fans. Hold fan blades still with a finger so they don't spin too fast. Don't use a vacuum inside the PC.
  • Check temps with a free tool like HWMonitor or HWiNFO. Consistently over 85-90°C under load = overheating.

B) Clicking, ticking, or grinding
Stop and pay attention here.

  • If it's coming from a traditional hard drive (HDD, not SSD): Back up your important files RIGHT NOW. Repeated clicking/ticking is often a sign a hard drive is failing. You can check health with CrystalDiskInfo (Windows).
  • If it's coming from a fan: A cable might be hitting a fan blade, or the fan bearing is worn out. With power off, open the side panel (desktop) and look for loose cables touching fans, and check for a wobbly fan.
  • Eject any CD/DVD/USB drive — sometimes it's just a disc spinning.

C) Rattling / vibration

  • Often a loose screw, side panel, or a desk vibrating. Gently press on the case — does it stop?
  • For desktops: Tighten case screws, make sure all fans and the hard drive are screwed in snugly, and make sure no cables are loose.
  • Move the PC to a flat, solid surface.

D) High-pitched whine / squeal, especially in games (coil whine)

  • This is usually harmless — it's electrical components vibrating under load, common on GPUs. It's annoying but not dangerous.
  • It often gets quieter if you cap your frame rate (turn on V-Sync) or enable Eco/Power Saver mode.

E) Beeping on startup, no Windows

  • Those are beep codes from the motherboard. Count them — e.g., 3 long, 2 short — and look up "[your computer model] beep codes." Usually means loose RAM or graphics card.

3. Quick fix checklist to try now

  1. Restart it — a stuck fan curve or runaway process often clears.
  2. Unplug everything except power, mouse/keyboard/monitor, and listen again. A bad external drive or speaker can fool you.
  3. Update your system and drivers — sometimes fan control is fixed by a BIOS update from the manufacturer.
  4. For a laptop: Try it on a hard table with the back slightly elevated for airflow.

    """Area of a circle: pi * r^2"""

    """Area of a rectangle: length * width"""
    return length * width

    return side ** 2

A classic Martini is simple — just gin (or vodka), dry vermouth, and a garnish. Here's how to make it perfect:

### The Classic Gin Martini

**You'll need:**
* Martini glass or coupe, mixing glass, bar spoon, jigger, and strainer
* Lots of ice
* 2 1/2 oz (75ml) good-quality gin - like Tanqueray, Beefeater, Hendricks, or The Botanist
* 1/2 oz (15ml) dry vermouth - like Dolin Dry or Noilly Prat
* Garnish: green olives on a pick OR a lemon twist
* Optional: 1-2 dashes orange bitters

That’s a 5:1 ratio, which is the classic starting point.

**Steps:**

**1. Chill your glass**
Fill your martini glass with ice and water and set it aside while you mix. A cold glass is non-negotiable.

**2. Mix it**
Dump the ice water out of your mixing glass and fill it 2/3 full with fresh ice. Add the vermouth first, then the gin.

**3. Stir it**
Stir gently with a bar spoon for about 30 seconds. You want it ice-cold and slightly diluted, not watery. Stirring keeps it silky clear — that's traditional for a Martini.

> Want it shaken like James Bond? Add everything to a cocktail shaker with ice and shake hard for 10-15 seconds. It will be colder, more diluted, and a little cloudy.

**4. Strain and garnish**
Empty your chilled glass (dump the ice water). Strain the martini into it.
For olives: drop in 1-3 green olives.
For a twist: cut a 1-inch strip of lemon peel, squeeze it over the drink to release the oils, rub it around the rim, then drop it in.

That's it. Serve immediately.

### Easy Variations

Once you have the classic down, adjust to taste:

* **Dry Martini:** Use less vermouth. Try 1/4 oz (7ml) or just rinse the glass with vermouth and dump it out.
* **Wet / 50-50:** Use equal parts gin and vermouth. 1 1/2 oz gin + 1 1/2 oz vermouth. Very smooth.
* **Vodka Martini:** Swap gin for vodka (Tito's, Grey Goose, Ketel One). Same ratio. Usually garnished with olives.
* **Dirty Martini:** Add 1/4 to 1/2 oz olive brine along with the gin/vermouth. Garnish with olives.
* **Gibson:** Garnish with 2 cocktail onions instead of olives.

### 3 Pro Tips for a Better Martini

1. **Keep your vermouth fresh.** It's wine! Once opened, keep it in the fridge and use within 1-2 months, or it will taste stale.
2. **Use great ice.** Big, solid cubes melt slower and chill without over-diluting.
3. **Keep gin/vodka in the freezer.** A super-cold base makes for an extra-crisp martini.

If you're of legal drinking age, enjoy responsibly — martinis are strong! Want a recipe for a Dirty, Espresso Martini, or Vodka version next?

To reset your password, it depends a bit on which account / app you mean — but almost all sites follow the same process:

### Quick way (if you're logged out)

1. **Go to the Login page** for that website or app
2. Look for **"Forgot password?" / "Reset password" / "Can't sign in?"** under the login button and click it
3. **Enter the email address** (or username / phone number) you signed up with
4. Check your email for a password reset link — check Spam / Junk / Promotions too. It usually arrives within a few minutes and expires in 1-24 hours.
5. Click the link in the email and **create a new password**
6. Log back in with your new password

Pick a strong new password: at least 12+ characters, unique to that site, with a mix of letters, numbers, and symbols. A password manager makes this much easier.

### If you're already logged in and just want to change it

Go to **Settings > Account / Security / Password > Change Password**. You'll usually need to enter your current password first, then the new one twice.

### Not getting the reset email?

* Double-check you typed the email correctly — try any other emails you might have used
* Check Spam, Junk, Trash, and Promotions / Updates tabs
* Wait 5-10 minutes and click **Resend**
* If you no longer have access to that email, look for **"Need more help?"** on the reset page to contact their Support team — they'll usually ask you to verify your identity

Let me know which service / app you're trying to reset (like Gmail, Apple, Instagram, etc.) and I can give you the exact steps for that one.

I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice, just general information:

**If you mean this chat with me:**
You can save, copy, or screenshot the text for personal use. I don't have privacy rights like a person does. Just be careful if you publish it publicly and it contains your own personal information.

**If you mean recording a conversation with other people:**
That's where the law gets tricky.

1. **Are you part of the conversation?**
In most places you have to be a participant to legally record. Secretly recording / eavesdropping on a conversation you're *not* part of is almost always illegal.

2. **One-party vs. all-party consent:**
* **U.S. Federal law:** generally requires only *one-party* consent — meaning if *you* consent to the recording, it's okay federally.
* **U.S. States:** About 35+ states follow one-party consent, but about 10-12 states require *all-party / two-party* consent — everyone being recorded must know and agree. That includes places like California, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Montana, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Washington, among others.
If people are in different states, the strictest rule is safest to follow.

* **UK:** You can generally record a conversation you're part of for your own use, but sharing it or playing it to third parties has extra rules under data protection / privacy law.
* **Canada, Australia, EU:** Generally require consent of a participant and have strong privacy / GDPR-type rules about sharing, storing, and publishing recordings, especially at work.

3. **Do you have to announce it?**
Safest practice everywhere is to get clear consent upfront: "Is it okay if I record this for my notes?" For phone/customer service calls, that "this call may be recorded" disclaimer is how companies do it.

In-person, some all-party states also require consent to be explicit, not just implied.

When in doubt:
- Tell everyone you're recording and what it's for
- Get a yes on the recording itself
- Don't record confidential settings (doctor, lawyer, workplace HR, bathrooms/locker rooms, etc.) without specific advice
- Don't publish or post the recording without thinking about privacy law

Changing your car's engine oil is a great DIY job — it takes about 30-45 minutes once you have the supplies. Here's the general process:

> **Important:** Always check your owner's manual first for your specific car — it tells you the right oil type/viscosity (like 5W-30), how much oil it takes, what filter to use, and torque specs. If you're not comfortable getting under a car, have a shop do it.

### What you'll need
1. Correct amount and type of new engine oil for your car
2. New oil filter for your car
3. New drain plug crush washer / gasket (most cars need this)
4. Socket wrench, oil filter wrench, funnel
5. Oil drain pan (with a lid for transport)
6. Jack + jack stands or ramps, wheel chocks, parking brake on
7. Gloves, safety glasses, rags/cardboard, torque wrench if you have one

Park on a flat, level surface.

### 1. Prep the car
1. Start the engine for 1-2 minutes to warm the oil slightly — warm oil drains faster. Don't do it when fully hot, you can get burned.
2. Turn car off, put in Park (or in gear), set parking brake, chock wheels.
3. If you need to lift it, jack it up and place it securely on **jack stands or ramps**. Never work under a car held up by just a jack.

Open the hood, remove the engine oil filler cap on top of the engine. This helps it drain.

### 2. Drain the old oil
1. Put the drain pan under the oil drain plug (under the engine oil pan).
2. With a socket wrench, loosen the drain plug counter-clockwise. Finish unscrewing by hand, keeping pressure in so oil doesn't spray early.
3. Pull the plug away quickly and let the oil drain completely — usually 5-10 minutes until it's just dripping.
4. Check the drain plug and replace the crush washer. Wipe clean, then reinstall the plug by hand first to avoid cross-threading, then snug with a wrench. Don't overtighten — check manual, often around 25-30 ft-lbs.

### 3. Change the oil filter
1. Move the drain pan under the oil filter.
2. Loosen the filter with an oil filter wrench and unscrew by hand. It will be full of oil, so keep it upright.
3. Let it drain, then wipe the mounting surface clean on the engine.
4. Dab a little fresh oil on the rubber gasket of the *new* filter with your finger. This helps it seal.
5. Screw the new filter on by hand until the gasket contacts, then another 3/4 turn by hand. Most filters say hand-tight only — don't use the wrench to tighten.

### 4. Add new oil
1. Place a funnel in the filler hole on top of the engine.
2. Pour in the amount from your manual — but pour about 1/2 quart *less* than full capacity to start.
3. Replace the filler cap, wait a minute, then check the dipstick: pull it out, wipe it, reinsert fully, pull out again. Add a little more at a time until it's between the MIN and MAX / dots, closer to MAX but not over.
4. Put filler cap back on and dipstick back in.

### 5. Check for leaks and finish
1. Start the engine and let it run 30-60 seconds. Check under the car and around the filter and drain plug for leaks. The oil pressure light should go off.
2. Turn off engine, wait 1-2 minutes for oil to settle, re-check dipstick and top off if needed.
3. If your car has an oil life / maintenance reminder, reset it per your manual.
4. Write down the mileage and date for your next change.

### 6. Clean up properly
Pour the used oil from the drain pan into the old oil bottles using a funnel. Put the old filter in a plastic bag. Take both to an auto parts store, dealership, or municipal recycling center — most take it for free.

**Do NOT** pour oil down a drain, on the ground, or in the trash. One oil change can contaminate a huge amount of water.

---

Quick tips:
* If the drain plug or filter won't budge, or you see stripped threads, metal shavings in the oil, or milky oil, stop and get a mechanic — those can be signs of a bigger problem.
* Most modern cars with full synthetic go 5,000 - 10,000 miles between changes — go by your manual, not just the 3,000-mile sticker.

Changing your car's engine oil is a great DIY job — it takes about 30-45 minutes once you have the supplies. Here's the general process:

Important: Always check your owner's manual first for your specific car — it tells you the right oil type/viscosity (like 5W-30), how much oil it takes, what filter to use, and torque specs. If you're not comfortable getting under a car, have a shop do it.

What you'll need

  1. Correct amount and type of new engine oil for your car
  2. New oil filter for your car
  3. New drain plug crush washer / gasket (most cars need this)
  4. Socket wrench, oil filter wrench, funnel
  5. Oil drain pan (with a lid for transport)
  6. Jack + jack stands or ramps, wheel chocks, parking brake on
  7. Gloves, safety glasses, rags/cardboard, torque wrench if you have one

Park on a flat, level surface.

1. Prep the car

  1. Start the engine for 1-2 minutes to warm the oil slightly — warm oil drains faster. Don't do it when fully hot, you can get burned.
  2. Turn car off, put in Park (or in gear), set parking brake, chock wheels.
  3. If you need to lift it, jack it up and place it securely on jack stands or ramps. Never work under a car held up by just a jack.

Open the hood, remove the engine oil filler cap on top of the engine. This helps it drain.

2. Drain the old oil

  1. Put the drain pan under the oil drain plug (under the engine oil pan).
  2. With a socket wrench, loosen the drain plug counter-clockwise. Finish unscrewing by hand, keeping pressure in so oil doesn't spray early.
  3. Pull the plug away quickly and let the oil drain completely — usually 5-10 minutes until it's just dripping.
  4. Check the drain plug and replace the crush washer. Wipe clean, then reinstall the plug by hand first to avoid cross-threading, then snug with a wrench. Don't overtighten — check manual, often around 25-30 ft-lbs.

3. Change the oil filter

  1. Move the drain pan under the oil filter.
  2. Loosen the filter with an oil filter wrench and unscrew by hand. It will be full of oil, so keep it upright.
  3. Let it drain, then wipe the mounting surface clean on the engine.
  4. Dab a little fresh oil on the rubber gasket of the new filter with your finger. This helps it seal.
  5. Screw the new filter on by hand until the gasket contacts, then another 3/4 turn by hand. Most filters say hand-tight only — don't use the wrench to tighten.

4. Add new oil

  1. Place a funnel in the filler hole on top of the engine.
  2. Pour in the amount from your manual — but pour about 1/2 quart less than full capacity to start.
  3. Replace the filler cap, wait a minute, then check the dipstick: pull it out, wipe it, reinsert fully, pull out again. Add a little more at a time until it's between the MIN and MAX / dots, closer to MAX but not over.
  4. Put filler cap back on and dipstick back in.

5. Check for leaks and finish

  1. Start the engine and let it run 30-60 seconds. Check under the car and around the filter and drain plug for leaks. The oil pressure light should go off.
  2. Turn off engine, wait 1-2 minutes for oil to settle, re-check dipstick and top off if needed.
  3. If your car has an oil life / maintenance reminder, reset it per your manual.
  4. Write down the mileage and date for your next change.

6. Clean up properly

Pour the used oil from the drain pan into the old oil bottles using a funnel. Put the old filter in a plastic bag. Take both to an auto parts store, dealership, or municipal recycling center — most take it for free.

Do NOT pour oil down a drain, on the ground, or in the trash. One oil change can contaminate a huge amount of water.

Quick tips:

  • If the drain plug or filter won't budge, or you see stripped threads, metal shavings in the oil, or milky oil, stop and get a mechanic — those can be signs of a bigger problem.
  • Most modern cars with full synthetic go 5,000 - 10,000 miles between changes — go by your manual, not just the 3,000-mile sticker.
